learning.reason: Elastic Throughput adjusts throughput to actual demand, so unpredictable peaks do not need to be provisioned in advance.
learning.concept: Throughput modes determine how a file system handles changes in workload. Storage classes address data access frequency and storage cost.

title: Reduce network latency between compute nodes in the same AZ
prompt: A time-limited simulation runs in a single AZ. The EC2 workers use supported instance types from the same generation, and they frequently exchange intermediate results from every compute step among all workers. Low latency and high throughput between workers are the top priority, ahead of fault isolation across AZs. Which EC2 placement is appropriate?

choices.text: Place each instance on a different rack in a spread placement group.
choices.explanation: This placement prioritizes isolating individual nodes from failures; it does not meet the requirement to place the compute nodes close together.

choices.text: Split the workers across multiple partitions in a partition placement group.
choices.explanation: This is suited to isolating racks across partitions, but it does not place all workers close together for low latency.

choices.text: Place all workers in a cluster placement group in the same AZ.
choices.explanation: This placement prioritizes low-latency, high-bandwidth communication between nodes within a single AZ.

choices.text: Create an Auto Scaling group in the same AZ without specifying a placement group.
choices.explanation: This limits the group to an AZ, but specifying an Auto Scaling group alone does not select close placement for the nodes.

source.label: Amazon EC2 — プレイスメントグループの配置戦略

learning.reason: A cluster placement group prioritizes low-latency, high-throughput communication between instances in a single AZ.
learning.concept: Placement strategies serve different purposes even within the same AZ. Spread and partition placement groups limit the scope of correlated failures.

title: Validate backup restore results while keeping the production EFS file system intact
prompt: An EFS file system is protected daily with AWS Backup. Auditors require a monthly test that creates an isolated, new file system from a recovery point, confirms that application tests can read it, and records the results. The decision to restore to production is handled by a separate gate, and test resources are cleaned up after verification. Which approach centered on AWS Backup reduces operational work?

choices.text: Save notifications for successful backup jobs and counts of recovery points that are not corrupted as audit logs.
choices.explanation: This is evidence that backups succeeded; it does not prove that the application can read restored files.

choices.text: Use a restore testing plan to restore EFS on a schedule, attempt reads within the specified validation window, and record the validation results.
choices.explanation: This tests behavior on a restore resource separate from production and can use AWS Backup to schedule the test and clean up when it ends.

choices.text: Add a copy to a separate vault in the backup plan and treat completion of both copies as a successful file-read test.
choices.explanation: Copying provides a separate backup, but does not by itself perform a restore test or have the application read the files.

choices.text: Replicate a secondary EFS file system daily and save the replication completion notification as the validation result for a recovery point.
choices.explanation: Replication does not confirm that a specified AWS Backup recovery point can be read.

source.label: AWS Backup — 復元テスト

learning.reason: A restore testing plan manages the schedule and restores a new EFS file system into a validation environment. The validation process records read results, and test resources are cleaned up after the test.
learning.concept: Completion of a restore job and confirmation that an application can use the restored data are separate checks.

title: Keep existing capacity available while adding distribution to a new AZ
prompt: A new AZ has been added to an EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an ALB. Until just before the change, healthy instances were only in the original AZ, and the group's desired and maximum capacities are equal. The service requirement is not to reduce existing capacity before rebalancing. Spot is not used, and an even distribution across AZs is preferred. Which behavior should be used?

choices.text: Disable AZRebalance and lower only the CPU threshold for target tracking to place the same number of instances in each AZ.
choices.explanation: Target tracking adjusts desired capacity based on load. Disabling rebalancing does not directly correct the distribution of existing capacity after adding an AZ.

choices.text: Manually terminate instances in the original AZ first, then restore capacity by adding new instances.
choices.explanation: This creates a shortfall and waits for new instances to launch, so it does not meet the requirement to avoid reducing existing capacity first.

choices.text: Use AZRebalance to launch instances in the new AZ first, then gradually terminate instances in the original AZ.
choices.explanation: Even near the maximum capacity, a temporary overage is allowed so the group can launch first and correct the imbalance.

choices.text: Enable Capacity Rebalancing for Spot and wait for a replacement event to launch instances in the new AZ.
choices.explanation: Responding to Spot interruption risk and rebalancing On-Demand instances across AZs are different purposes.

source.label: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling — AZ間の再均衡

learning.reason: During AZ rebalancing, Auto Scaling launches instances first in the AZ with fewer instances, then terminates instances in the AZ with more. It can temporarily exceed maximum capacity when needed.
learning.concept: AZRebalance corrects imbalances across AZs. Spot Capacity Rebalancing replaces Spot capacity that is at higher risk of interruption.

sourceLabel: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling — AZ rebalancing

title: Add a time-based SLA and over-threshold notifications to cross-Region replication
prompt: Replication is already configured between two general purpose S3 buckets in the same account, each in a different Region. A service level with an SLA is now required to replicate at least 99.9% of eligible new audit objects within 15 minutes during each monthly billing period, along with object-level notifications when that threshold is exceeded. Which change should be made, assuming the workload stays within the specified conditions and service limits?

choices.text: Enable S3 RTC and send replication threshold-exceeded events to a notification destination.
choices.explanation: This combines a replication mode with an SLA and notifications that identify the affected objects.

choices.text: Enable replication metrics for standard CRR only and assume that a 15-minute SLA is added automatically.
choices.explanation: Metrics let you monitor status, but metrics alone do not add an SLA for replication time.

choices.text: Run S3 Batch Replication as an equivalent 15-minute process and produce a job completion report.
choices.explanation: It can be used to process existing or previously unreplicated objects, but it does not configure a 15-minute SLA for each new object.

choices.text: Receive PutObject events through an S3 event notification from the source and treat them as confirmation that replication has completed.
choices.explanation: A write event on the source does not indicate completion of replication to the destination or that the time threshold has been exceeded.

source.label: Amazon S3 — Replication Time Control

learning.reason: Enable S3 RTC in the replication rule and send a replication event notification when the 15-minute threshold is exceeded.
learning.concept: S3 RTC provides an SLA for the replication time of new objects. Enabling replication metrics alone does not add an SLA.

title: Return SQS failed messages at a controlled rate after fixing the cause
prompt: A worker processes a standard SQS queue, and messages that repeatedly fail are moved to its associated dead-letter queue (DLQ). The cause has been fixed, so the messages need to be returned to the original queue. New messages are also being processed, so the load must be controlled with a fixed maximum move rate. Which design avoids a custom redrive worker?

choices.text: Increase the original queue's maxReceiveCount and wait for messages already in the DLQ to return to the original queue.
choices.explanation: The receive-count condition determines when messages will be sent to the DLQ in the future. It does not restore messages that have already arrived there.

choices.text: Configure the DLQ as a reverse dead-letter queue for the original queue and infer a fixed rate from the database connection limit.
choices.explanation: A DLQ configuration triggered by receive failures is not an operation for restoring existing messages at an arbitrary rate.

choices.text: Start SQS redrive from the DLQ, set the original queue as the destination, and specify the maximum rate the workload can handle.
choices.explanation: This returns messages to the original queue without custom processing. Specifying a maximum rate helps limit the load on normal processing.

choices.text: Adjust the DLQ's visibility timeout to automatically move messages back to the original queue.
choices.explanation: The visibility timeout makes messages visible again in the same queue; it does not transfer them to the original queue.

source.label: Amazon SQS — デッドレターキューの再処理

learning.reason: Use SQS dead-letter queue redrive to move messages back to the original queue and set a maximum rate.
learning.concept: The condition for moving messages from the original queue to a DLQ is separate from the operation that restores them. You can set a rate limit during redrive to manage load.

title: Use a readable standby and automatic failover in one Region
prompt: A supported version of RDS for PostgreSQL is in use. If one Availability Zone in a single Region becomes unavailable, writes must be restored without an administrator promoting a replica. Under normal conditions, the standby must also serve read-only queries, and read clients need a shared connection endpoint. Migration of the data to Amazon Aurora is not allowed. Which configuration should be selected?

choices.text: Use an RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster, with the writer endpoint for writes and the reader endpoint for reads.
choices.explanation: The reader handles reads under normal conditions and automatically becomes the writer in another Availability Zone if the writer fails.

choices.text: Use an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance and make the standby instance the application's shared read endpoint.
choices.explanation: Automatic failover is available, but reads from the standby are not supported during normal operation.

choices.text: Add a standard read replica in another Availability Zone to a single-AZ RDS instance and let RDS promote it automatically if the primary fails.
choices.explanation: A standard read replica can serve reads, but this configuration alone does not provide managed automatic failover.

choices.text: Enable RDS point-in-time recovery and restore a recent snapshot if the primary becomes unavailable.
choices.explanation: This operational approach creates a restored instance; it does not meet both normal read requirements and automatic failover.

source.label: Amazon RDS — Multi-AZ DBクラスター

learning.reason: A reader in an RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster can serve reads and support automatic failover.
learning.concept: The standby in an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance is not used for reads. A reader in a Multi-AZ DB cluster has a reader endpoint.

title: Prepare custom event ingestion for a Regional failure
prompt: Rules and targets that process the same workload have already been deployed to EventBridge custom event buses in two Regions. An external sending application uses a supported AWS SDK. When an issue with the primary is detected, you want subsequent custom events to be sent to the secondary without requiring the sender to switch Regions individually. The receiving side can tolerate reprocessing. Which configuration should you use?

choices.text: Add retry settings to the target of the primary event rule, and continue using the primary Region API from the sending application.
choices.explanation: Retries for a target do not change the destination Region of the API used to submit events.

choices.text: Configure a secondary DLQ for the primary target and assume that it will receive events even when event submission fails.
choices.explanation: A DLQ for target processing failures does not handle an API failure before the event is submitted to the bus.

choices.text: Create custom buses with the same name in the primary and secondary Regions, so that PutEvents specifying that name automatically sends events to the other Region.
choices.explanation: Creating buses with the same name does not add failover behavior to a Region-specific API call.

choices.text: Configure a global endpoint and a Route 53 health check, and specify that endpoint ID in PutEvents from the sending application.
choices.explanation: This abstracts the submission destination for the sending application and can send events to the secondary bus when the primary has an issue.

source.label: Amazon EventBridge — グローバルエンドポイント

learning.reason: Associate two Regional buses and a Route 53 health check with an EventBridge global endpoint. The sender uses that endpoint with PutEvents.
learning.concept: A global endpoint switches the ingestion destination for custom events. Processing rules and targets downstream are operated in each Region.

title: Centrally control and log VPC name resolution
prompt: Several application VPCs all use the Amazon-provided Route 53 VPC Resolver for name resolution. The security team wants the VPCs to reject queries for specified domains and send investigation logs for both allowed and denied queries to a central destination. Agents cannot be installed on individual EC2 instances. Which two configurations are required?

choices.text: Associate only Route 53 Resolver query logging, and assume that queries for the specified domains are denied once log delivery begins.
choices.explanation: Query logging records queries. A separate rule is required to block domains.

choices.text: Associate a DNS Firewall rule group that blocks the specified domains with the target VPCs.
choices.explanation: The Resolver in each target VPC can match the domain list and deny the relevant queries.

choices.text: Enable flow logs for each VPC and use a destination IP filter in the flow logs as a DNS deny list.
choices.explanation: Flow log filters select which traffic to record; they do not evaluate domain names in queries and deny them.

choices.text: Associate a Resolver query logging configuration with the target VPCs and send the logs to a central destination.
choices.explanation: You can investigate the queries recorded by Resolver together with DNS Firewall evaluation information.

choices.text: Restrict application HTTPS destinations with security groups and use them to control Resolver queries by domain name as well.
choices.explanation: Controls based on IP addresses and ports do not replace denying queries for specified domains through the Amazon-provided Resolver.

source.label: Amazon Route 53 — Resolver DNS Firewall

learning.reason: Associate a DNS Firewall rule group with the target VPCs to control destinations queried through Resolver. Separately associate Resolver query logging to collect investigation records.
learning.concept: DNS Firewall controls DNS queries by domain name. Resolver query logging provides the investigation records.

title: Continuously assess images in production repositories
prompt: A private ECR registry has production repositories whose names begin with prod- and development repositories whose names begin with dev-. Images are currently scanned when pushed. For production only, you want the corresponding stored images to be automatically reassessed when new vulnerabilities are published. Keep scan-on-push for development, and do not set up a scheduled process that pushes production images again. Which configuration should you use?

choices.text: Apply basic scan-on-push to the entire registry and assume that production images that have not been updated will also be reassessed automatically.
choices.explanation: Scan-on-push alone does not meet the requirement to continuously assess images against new vulnerabilities when they are not pushed again.

choices.text: Enable enhanced scanning and configure every repository for scan-on-push only.
choices.explanation: Enabling enhanced scanning does not provide continuous assessment of production images when the setting is scan-on-push only.

choices.text: Configure enhanced scanning for the registry, with continuous scanning for prod- and scan-on-push for dev-.
choices.explanation: This applies continuous assessment to the production repositories while limiting development repositories to scan-on-push.

choices.text: Set all repositories to continuous enhanced scanning and hide only the findings from development repositories.
choices.explanation: Hiding findings does not prevent continuous assessment from running on development repositories.

source.label: Amazon ECR — 拡張スキャン

learning.reason: Use enhanced scanning filters to continuously scan production repositories and scan development repositories when images are pushed.
learning.concept: Registry-level ECR enhanced scanning integrates with Amazon Inspector. You can choose a scan frequency based on repository matching criteria.

title: Require TLS for application connections to existing PostgreSQL
prompt: An RDS for PostgreSQL instance migrating from an older major version currently has rds.force_ssl set to 0 in its custom parameter group. Separately from the HTTPS frontend, you want to limit connections from applications in the VPC to the existing database port to TLS. Which approach makes the database reject new clients that are misconfigured to use plaintext?

choices.text: Change only the approved applications to use TLS verification settings and leave rds.force_ssl=0 on the database.
choices.explanation: The approved applications can use TLS, but the database will not reject misconfigured clients.

choices.text: Set rds.force_ssl to 1 in the custom DB parameter group and plan any restart needed to apply it. Configure the applications to verify the certificate using the appropriate CA.
choices.explanation: This makes the database reject plaintext connections and lets clients verify the certificate of the endpoint they connect to.

choices.text: Keep the database parameter unchanged and add only TCP port 443 to the database security group for TLS.
choices.explanation: PostgreSQL uses the existing database port for TLS. Adding port 443 cannot require TLS on that port.

choices.text: Restrict only the route to the database to private subnets and leave the database parameter unchanged.
choices.explanation: Even over an authorized route, an application can still initiate a plaintext connection.

source.label: Amazon RDS — PostgreSQLでのSSL/TLS

learning.reason: Require TLS through the RDS DB parameter group and configure application connections on the existing port to verify the certificate.
learning.concept: PostgreSQL negotiates TLS over its regular database port. Network permission to a port and enforcement of TLS are separate controls.

title: Reject unencrypted mounts to an existing EFS file system
prompt: An existing EFS file system is encrypted at rest and mounted over NFS by EC2 instances in the same VPC. You must preserve the application paths, and all clients must encrypt data in transit from now on. You also want EFS itself to reject clients that mistakenly use plaintext NFS. Which two measures are required?

choices.text: Change the EC2 mount configuration to use the tls option of the EFS mount helper.
choices.explanation: A correctly configured client can then mount the same file system with encryption in transit.

choices.text: Rotate the EFS at-rest encryption key so that new mounts automatically use TLS with the same key.
choices.explanation: Rotating the key that protects stored data does not encrypt NFS traffic between the client and EFS.

choices.text: Limit the EFS security group to TCP 2049 and assume it can reject plaintext connections arriving on the same port.
choices.explanation: A security group does not evaluate whether a client using the same port is using TLS.

choices.text: Fix the POSIX user with an access point and assume that clients not using TLS will lack mount permissions.
choices.explanation: POSIX user settings alone do not enforce encryption in transit.

choices.text: Explicitly deny client mounts in the file system policy when aws:SecureTransport is false.
choices.explanation: This condition lets EFS reject connections that are not encrypted in transit.

source.label: Amazon EFS — NFSクライアントへのIAMアクセス制御

learning.reason: Enable TLS through the EFS mount helper and block connections without TLS using an explicit deny in the file system policy.
learning.concept: EFS encryption at rest and TLS serve different purposes. The aws:SecureTransport condition in a file system policy can require TLS for client connections.

sourceLabel: Amazon EFS — IAM access control for NFS clients

title: Granting an on-premises job temporary AWS permissions with an existing PKI
prompt: An unattended on-premises job has an X.509 certificate issued by the corporate CA. It needs to use an IAM role that can write only to a specified S3 prefix. Do not store long-term access keys with the job or require interactive employee sign-in. Which design uses the trust in the existing certificate?

choices.text: Assign a permission set to an employee group in IAM Identity Center and have the job obtain credentials through an employee's interactive sign-in each time.
choices.explanation: This does not meet the requirements for unattended execution or using the existing workload's X.509 certificate.

choices.text: Grant the IAM role write access to S3 and send only the corporate CA certificate directly to STS AssumeRole.
choices.explanation: A call to general AssumeRole does not authenticate directly with a corporate certificate. The certificate must be exchanged for AWS credentials.

choices.text: Store long-term IAM access keys in Secrets Manager and have the job retrieve them as static credentials at startup.
choices.explanation: Adding a secret-storage mechanism does not let the existing certificate replace long-term credentials.

choices.text: Configure a trust anchor for the corporate CA and a profile in IAM Roles Anywhere, then obtain temporary credentials for a narrowly scoped IAM role that trusts the service.
choices.explanation: This issues temporary credentials based on the existing certificate, while the S3 permissions can be restricted to the intended prefix.

source.label: AWS IAM Roles Anywhere — 短期認証情報

learning.reason: Register the corporate CA as a trust anchor in Roles Anywhere and configure the role's trust policy and a profile. The job writes to S3 using temporary credentials based on its certificate.
learning.concept: The certificate verifies the identity of an external workload. The IAM role associated with temporary credentials limits what it can do in S3.

sourceLabel: AWS IAM Roles Anywhere — Temporary credentials

title: Granting Partial S3 Access by Corporate Directory Group
prompt: Analysts in multiple departments are synchronized from an existing corporate IdP to IAM Identity Center. The applications requesting access support trusted identity propagation. In an S3 data lake, analysts should use temporary credentials to read only the prefixes authorized for their department, and access should reflect group changes when they transfer between departments. Which configuration should you choose without listing individual names in the bucket policy?

choices.text: Associate an S3 Access Grants instance with Identity Center, then configure the permitted prefixes for each department group in the registered S3 locations.
choices.explanation: Combining synchronized group membership with S3 locations lets Access Grants issue temporary credentials scoped to the requested access.

choices.text: Have all employees assume the same IAM role and grant that role GetObject access to every prefix.
choices.explanation: Permissions on a shared role alone cannot restrict each employee's access based on department.

choices.text: Create a separate S3 access point for each department, but let every department use all access points through the same shared role.
choices.explanation: Separating access points alone does not establish access permissions based on group membership.

choices.text: Keep Identity Center synchronization enabled and specify corporate directory group names directly as the Principal in the S3 bucket policy.
choices.explanation: A directory group name cannot be specified directly as a bucket policy Principal in this way.

source.label: Amazon S3 — Access Grantsと企業ディレクトリID

learning.reason: Integrate S3 Access Grants with IAM Identity Center and grant department groups access to permitted prefixes within registered S3 locations.
learning.concept: Corporate directory identities are referenced through their identities synchronized with IAM Identity Center. Access Grants issues temporary access scoped to the permitted locations and prefixes.

sourceLabel: Amazon S3 — Access Grants and corporate directory identities

title: Apply built-in authentication protections according to risk
prompt: A Cognito user pool on the Plus plan provides sign-in with usernames and passwords. MFA is optional in the user pool, and the target users have not yet enabled MFA. Do not require additional steps for low-risk sign-ins, but apply an MFA challenge or block sign-in according to risks detected by Cognito. The required sign-in flow and client information are available. Which approach meets these requirements without implementing custom risk assessment?

choices.text: Configure the user pool to use MFA conditionally, then use adaptive authentication in Threat protection to configure MFA or blocking based on risk.
choices.explanation: Built-in risk assessment can apply the configured actions during sign-in.

choices.text: Leave Threat protection in audit mode and only log the detected risks.
choices.explanation: Audit mode records findings but does not apply additional authentication or block sign-in.

choices.text: Require MFA for the entire user pool at every sign-in and do not configure risk-based actions.
choices.explanation: This adds a step to routine sign-ins and does not meet the requirement to strengthen authentication only at higher risk.

choices.text: Select IAM roles by risk in the Cognito identity pool and leave user pool authentication unchanged.
choices.explanation: Identity pool role selection concerns AWS temporary credentials; it does not apply MFA or deny sign-in through user pool authentication.

source.label: Amazon Cognito — 適応認証

learning.reason: With MFA optional in the user pool, use Threat protection adaptive authentication in enforcement mode and configure an action for each risk level.
learning.concept: Risk-based MFA challenges or blocks are configured as adaptive authentication actions. With Require MFA, users who have not configured an MFA method are blocked. Once a user enables MFA, they receive an MFA challenge regardless of adaptive authentication risk settings.

title: Protecting new audit logs with a specified KMS key
prompt: Create a new CloudWatch Logs log group for sensitive data. An operator role must be able to work with the logs, but its permitted KMS use must be limited to calls that CloudWatch Logs makes on its behalf. The default encryption with an existing AWS-owned key does not meet the audit requirement for a customer key. Which configuration should you use?

choices.text: Do not associate a key with the log group, and allow the operator role to use the KMS key directly.
choices.explanation: Granting the user key permissions alone does not make CloudWatch Logs use that key for encryption at rest.

choices.text: Associate the key with the log group and allow the operator role to make unconditional direct calls to the same key.
choices.explanation: This selects a customer key but does not limit the operator role's KMS use to calls through Logs.

choices.text: Associate the KMS key with the log group and configure the required key policy for CloudWatch Logs. Limit the operator role's related KMS permissions to Logs in the same Region using kms:ViaService.
choices.explanation: The storage key is specified, and authorization conditions can distinguish service proxy calls from direct calls by the operator role.

choices.text: Use TLS only for log ingestion and do not associate a key with CloudWatch Logs.
choices.explanation: This protects data in transit but does not meet the requirement to use a customer-managed key at rest.

source.label: Amazon CloudWatch Logs — KMSによる暗号化

learning.reason: Associate a customer managed KMS key with the log group and grant the service the required key permissions. Add a service-mediated condition to the operator role's KMS permissions.
learning.concept: Distinguish CloudWatch Logs default encryption from an explicitly selected KMS key. kms:ViaService can condition access on a request being made through a supported service.

sourceLabel: Amazon CloudWatch Logs — Encryption with KMS

title: Authenticate with the application role without distributing a DB password
prompt: An application on ECS connects to a compatible RDS for PostgreSQL instance and authorizes each task using its task role. Business requirements prohibit storing or distributing a DB password to the application. New connections are infrequent, and you want to use short-lived tokens that are valid only when connecting, along with TLS. Keep the existing DB user's SQL privileges to a minimum. Which configuration should you use?

choices.text: Manage the DB password with Secrets Manager rotation, and have each task retrieve the password at startup.
choices.explanation: This reduces distribution of a fixed password, but the application still retrieves and uses the DB password to authenticate.

choices.text: Associate a KMS key with the RDS instance and allow kms:Decrypt for the task role.
choices.explanation: Permissions to encrypt and decrypt data are separate from permissions to log in to PostgreSQL.

choices.text: Allow rds:DescribeDBInstances for the task execution role and retain the current DB authentication method.
choices.explanation: This permission lets the role read instance information; it does not configure application tasks to authenticate as a DB user.

choices.text: Enable IAM DB authentication, grant rds_iam to the DB user, and grant the task role rds-db:connect for that user. Have tasks connect over TLS using short-lived tokens.
choices.explanation: This avoids distributing a long-lived password to the application and limits the task role's permission to connect as a specific DB user.

source.label: Amazon RDS — IAMデータベース認証

learning.reason: Enable IAM DB authentication and grant rds_iam to the PostgreSQL user. Allow the task role rds-db:connect for that user, then connect over TLS with a short-lived token.
learning.concept: IAM authentication tokens are valid for 15 minutes. The token is verified when the connection is established; the DB user's privileges determine SQL permissions after connecting.

title: Prevent administrators from shortening the retention of audit EBS backups
prompt: Use AWS Backup to separate EBS recovery points for auditing from operational backups used for other purposes. Allow a grace period for configuration review. After it ends, no one, including administrators in the management account, should be able to delete audit recovery points within the configured retention period or remove the protection provided by the lock. Which approach is required?

choices.text: Configure Vault Lock in Governance mode and allow users with existing strong administrative permissions to perform lock operations.
choices.explanation: In this mode, an administrator with sufficient permissions can change the lock, so it does not meet the requirement that even powerful administrators cannot remove it.

choices.text: Apply retention settings to backups in a dedicated vault, and configure Vault Lock in Compliance mode with a grace period.
choices.explanation: Once finalized, the protection cannot be removed using administrator permissions alone, and recovery points are protected according to a defined lifecycle.

choices.text: Apply a deny-delete policy to an operational role for the vault, while allowing management account administrators to change the policy at any time.
choices.explanation: This restricts ordinary operators, but does not protect against administrators who can change the policy.

choices.text: Copy backups to another vault periodically and set a retention period on the destination without using Vault Lock.
choices.explanation: This stores recovery points in a separate location, but administrators who are allowed to delete them can also change retention at the destination.

source.label: AWS Backup — Vault Lockのモード

learning.reason: Use a dedicated vault with Compliance mode Vault Lock and managed retention settings. After the grace period, ordinary administrator permissions cannot remove the lock.
learning.concept: Users with appropriate permissions can manage Vault Lock in Governance mode. Compliance mode allows changes during the grace period and provides immutability after it ends.

title: Renew an externally issued certificate while preserving its ALB association
prompt: A certificate from an external CA has been imported into ACM and is in use on an ALB HTTPS listener in the same Region. Before it expires, you receive a new certificate, private key, and intermediate certificates with the same subject name, key algorithm, and size, meeting ACM's reimport requirements. How can you renew the certificate without changing the ALB listener configuration or certificate ARN?

choices.text: Import the new certificate into ACM as a new certificate and wait for the ALB to switch automatically to the new ARN with the same subject name.
choices.explanation: A new import creates a different ARN. An existing ALB association does not move to that ARN based on the name alone.

choices.text: Request renewal from the external CA and wait for ACM managed renewal of the currently imported certificate.
choices.explanation: ACM does not perform managed renewal of imported external certificates.

choices.text: Specify the existing certificate ARN and reimport the new certificate, corresponding private key, and certificate chain into ACM.
choices.explanation: This updates the presented certificate while preserving the existing association between the ARN and the ALB listener.

choices.text: Remove the existing ACM certificate, associate the new certificate with the ALB, and then delete the old ARN.
choices.explanation: This can switch to the new certificate, but does not meet the requirement to retain the existing ARN and listener configuration.

source.label: AWS Certificate Manager — 証明書の再インポート

learning.reason: Reimporting with the existing ACM certificate ARN updates the certificate while preserving its association with the ALB.
learning.concept: ACM does not manage the renewal of certificates imported from external sources. Distinguish reimporting from importing a new certificate with a new ARN.

title: Reduce the cost of large sequential reads without relying on temporary credits
prompt: An EC2 analytics workload reads 5 TiB of data from an EBS volume sequentially and continuously, maintaining at least 150 MiB/s. The boot volume is separate, and there is little small random I/O. Measurements show that the instance has sufficient EBS bandwidth, and the HDD candidates cost less than SSDs. Assume all candidates have a capacity of 5 TiB. Which is the least expensive choice that meets the requirement without relying on bursting?

choices.text: Choose sc1 and configure it to exceed 150 MiB/s while bursting.
choices.explanation: A 5 TiB sc1 has a baseline of 60 MiB/s and cannot sustain the required throughput after bursting ends.

choices.text: Choose st1 and meet 150 MiB/s or more with baseline throughput.
choices.explanation: st1 provides baseline throughput of 40 MiB/s per TiB, or 200 MiB/s at 5 TiB.

choices.text: Choose gp3 and specify additional throughput to provide 150 MiB/s.
choices.explanation: This can meet the technical requirement, but SSD pricing is higher than st1, which also meets the conditions.

choices.text: Choose io2 and provision additional high IOPS for small I/O.
choices.explanation: This workload consists of large sequential I/O and does not require an expensive high-IOPS volume.

source.label: Amazon EBS — スループット最適化HDDとコールドHDD

learning.reason: At 5 TiB, st1 has baseline throughput of 200 MiB/s, so it meets the 150 MiB/s sequential-read requirement without bursting.
learning.concept: HDD capacity affects baseline throughput. For large sequential I/O, compare sustained bandwidth and price rather than deciding based only on maximum IOPS.

sourceLabel: Amazon EBS — Throughput Optimized HDD and Cold HDD

title: Choose an Aurora storage configuration based on total cost
prompt: The production Aurora PostgreSQL database has sustained, frequent I/O. With the current Aurora Standard configuration, instances and storage are estimated to cost 600 units per month, plus 400 units for read and write I/O. For the equivalent Aurora I/O-Optimized configuration, instances and storage are estimated to cost 850 units per month, with no additional charge for read and write I/O. Performance, data volume, and backup policy remain the same. Which option should you choose?

choices.text: Choose Standard because instances and storage total 600 units, excluding the 400 units for I/O.
choices.explanation: With Standard, you also pay for the read and write I/O described here, so 600 units is not the total cost.

choices.text: Keep Standard, assuming the current 400 units will still apply after switching to I/O-Optimized.
choices.explanation: In this estimate, I/O-Optimized has no separate charge for read and write I/O.

choices.text: Compare 850 units with Standard's total of 1,000 units, and move the cluster to I/O-Optimized.
choices.explanation: Under the assumption that performance and capacity remain unchanged, this reduces the total cost by 150 units.

choices.text: Keep Standard and stop only the billable I/O without stopping writes.
choices.explanation: There is no setting that stops charges for read and write I/O on Standard without changing the application.

source.label: Amazon Aurora — Auroraストレージの構成とI/O料金

learning.reason: For the same workload, Standard totals 1,000 units, while I/O-Optimized totals 850 units, making I/O-Optimized less expensive under this estimate.
learning.concept: Aurora I/O-Optimized does not charge separately for database read and write I/O. Because instance and storage rates also differ, compare the total cost.

sourceLabel: Amazon Aurora — Aurora storage configurations and I/O charges

title: Deliver compressed static files only to browsers that support them
prompt: You serve JavaScript and CSS from S3 through CloudFront, using supported sizes and MIME types. You cannot change the original files in S3 or their versioned URLs. For the new URLs in the next release, you want to reduce the amount of data transferred to browsers that support compression while preserving uncompressed content for browsers that do not. Both cases must use caching. Which two settings are required?

choices.text: Always declare Content-Encoding as br in a response headers policy, regardless of the viewer's capabilities.
choices.explanation: Declaring a header does not compress the original file. It also indicates the wrong format for unsupported browsers or uncompressed data.

choices.text: Enable compression for the target cache behavior.
choices.explanation: This configures the paths eligible for automatic compression by CloudFront.

choices.text: Disable compression in the cache policy, forward every value of Accept-Encoding to the origin, and have S3 compress files automatically.
choices.explanation: S3 does not automatically compress an uploaded uncompressed file for each request.

choices.text: Disable caching and rely only on origin compression settings.
choices.explanation: This does not meet the requirement to retain caching. The original files in S3 also cannot be changed.

choices.text: Enable Gzip and Brotli support for caching in the target cache policy.
choices.explanation: CloudFront can select a supported encoding based on the request, handle the format appropriately, and cache it.

source.label: Amazon CloudFront — 圧縮済みファイルの配信

learning.reason: Combine automatic compression for the target behavior with compression-format settings in the cache policy. CloudFront serves a format supported by the browser.
learning.concept: CloudFront uses Accept-Encoding to determine the compression format. The cache must also be configured to distinguish supported formats.

title: Detect spending that departs from seasonal patterns before reaching the monthly budget
prompt: Normal daily spending varies by day of the week. You want to detect when a service briefly costs more than usual, even if the monthly budget limit has not been reached, and get clues for investigating the cause. Which configuration sends notifications after billing data becomes available, without requiring you to update weekday-specific thresholds manually?

choices.text: Monitor the relevant scope with Cost Anomaly Detection and subscribe to alerts based on the detected amount.
choices.explanation: It can report anomalous spending in light of historical patterns and provide information to help investigate the cause.

choices.text: Use AWS Budgets to alert only when actual monthly spending reaches the limit.
choices.explanation: This does not meet the requirement to detect a temporary, unusual increase before the monthly limit is reached.

choices.text: Create a monthly saved report in Cost Explorer and manually compare each service with the previous month.
choices.explanation: This supports analysis but does not automatically estimate normal weekday variation and send notifications.

choices.text: Set a fixed CPU threshold in a CloudWatch alarm for a resource and use a breach as an alert for anomalous spending.
choices.explanation: A CPU increase does not correspond one-to-one with an anomalous billing-spend pattern.

source.label: AWS Cost Management — Cost Anomaly Detection

learning.reason: Use an AWS Cost Anomaly Detection monitor and notifications. It can detect spending that departs from historical patterns independently of a fixed monthly budget.
learning.concept: AWS Budgets alerts on exceeding a monetary target, while anomaly notifications detect deviations from normal spending patterns. These serve different purposes.

sourceLabel: AWS Cost Management — Cost Anomaly Detection

title: Run a non-interruptible Fargate service at Arm rates
prompt: An ECS Linux service runs on regular Fargate with x86_64, and Spot interruptions are not acceptable. In staging, you tested an Arm64 version with the same CPU, memory, and runtime, and confirmed that Arm64 is less expensive on regular Fargate in the target Region. The corresponding Fargate platform is available. Which two changes move production to this pricing configuration?

choices.text: Switch from regular Fargate to Fargate Spot and keep running x86_64.
choices.explanation: This could reduce cost, but it violates the requirement not to allow Spot interruptions.

choices.text: Tag the subnet for Arm64 in ECS and leave the image and task definition on x86_64.
choices.explanation: A subnet tag does not change a task's CPU architecture.

choices.text: Publish an Arm64 image, or a multi-architecture image that includes an Arm64 variant, to the registry.
choices.explanation: You must provide binaries and dependencies that run in an Arm64 environment.

choices.text: Set LINUX and ARM64 in runtimePlatform in the task definition, then replace the service with a new revision on regular Fargate.
choices.explanation: This changes the execution CPU and launches the task on regular Fargate with the corresponding pricing configuration.

choices.text: Set a different task CPU value to get Arm64 pricing while keeping the CPU architecture at x86_64.
choices.explanation: CPU quantity and architecture are separate settings. Changing CPU quantity does not switch execution to Arm64.

source.label: Amazon ECS — 64ビットARMのタスク定義

learning.reason: Publish a compatible image containing Arm64 binaries and configure the task definition for Arm64. Replace the tasks using regular Fargate capacity.
learning.concept: Fargate pricing varies by CPU architecture. The task's execution platform and container image architecture must match.

title: Reduce archive transition costs for large volumes of small logs
prompt: There are millions of analyzed log objects, each about 5 KB, generated daily. The original object keys do not need to be retained, and restoring the logs by day is sufficient. A new S3 Lifecycle configuration does not transition these small logs by default. Which approach will reduce storage costs while also reducing the number of per-object transition requests?

choices.text: Reapply the same default transition configuration without changing the object contents.
choices.explanation: As long as the objects fall under the default size restriction, the small objects will not be transitioned.

choices.text: Explicitly set the lifecycle size filter and transition every 5 KB object individually.
choices.explanation: This makes transitions possible, but it requires millions of transition requests and does not meet the requirement to reduce their number.

choices.text: Change each object's storage class with a separate copy operation.
choices.explanation: This changes objects one at a time and does not reduce the number of individual requests.

choices.text: Aggregate the logs into objects large enough to meet the transition requirements, one object per restoration day, then transition those objects with a lifecycle rule.
choices.explanation: The same information can be transitioned as fewer objects while preserving the requirement to restore logs by day.

source.label: Amazon S3 — ライフサイクルでの移行の制約

learning.reason: Create an archive for each day that is large enough, verify its completeness, and then clean up the original logs. Apply the transition to the aggregated objects.
learning.concept: By default, S3 Lifecycle does not transition objects smaller than 128 KB. Even when the size restriction is overridden, per-object transition request charges still apply.

title: Analyze S3 storage across the organization and incomplete multipart uploads
prompt: There are hundreds of S3 buckets across multiple AWS Organizations accounts. For cost analysis, you want to compare organization-wide storage trends, breakdowns for major high-capacity prefixes, and the capacity occupied by incomplete multipart uploads in an S3 dashboard. Which configuration avoids operating custom collection and aggregation jobs?

choices.text: Enable Inventory on each S3 bucket and display organization-wide trends, including incomplete parts, without custom aggregation.
choices.explanation: Inventory lists objects; it does not provide an organization-wide aggregation dashboard that includes incomplete parts.

choices.text: Configure an organization-level S3 Storage Lens dashboard with advanced metrics and prefix aggregation to compare the major areas.
choices.explanation: It can aggregate organization-wide usage and show storage amounts and optimization metrics for major prefixes.

choices.text: Enable bucket access logs alone and assume they will generate a storage trends dashboard without changing the log format.
choices.explanation: Access logs record requests; they do not aggregate capacity or incomplete parts.

choices.text: Display overall S3 service charges in Cost Explorer and read the capacity of incomplete parts for any prefix within a bucket.
choices.explanation: Service cost analysis and prefix-level storage metrics within S3 have different levels of granularity.

source.label: Amazon S3 — Storage Lensの組織およびプレフィックスの分析

learning.reason: Select the advanced metrics and prefix aggregation needed in an organization-level S3 Storage Lens dashboard to compare storage centrally.
learning.concept: Storage Lens aggregates storage and activity metrics across multiple accounts. S3 Inventory is a separate feature that outputs object-level listings.

sourceLabel: Amazon S3 — Storage Lens organization and prefix analysis

title: Manage the display deadline separately from DynamoDB physical deletion
prompt: There are tens of millions of temporary product notification records in DynamoDB. After its expiration, a record must no longer be displayed in the application, but physical deletion may take several days. You want to stop periodically running a Scan over all items and deleting them in a standard single-Region table. Each item's expiration time is determined individually. Choose two required measures.

choices.text: Store the expiration time for each item as an epoch time in seconds, and enable DynamoDB TTL on that attribute.
choices.explanation: This identifies expired items based on their individual expiration times. In a standard single-Region table, automatic deletion does not consume write capacity.

choices.text: After enabling TTL, leave the display logic unchanged because items are deleted immediately after they expire.
choices.explanation: Physical deletion may take time after expiration, so expired items can still be included in reads.

choices.text: In the application's read path, compare each item's expiration time with the current time and exclude items that are waiting for TTL deletion.
choices.explanation: This enforces the display deadline independently of physical deletion.

choices.text: Shorten the PITR retention period and assume that this will delete each item from the current table after it expires.
choices.explanation: PITR retains history for restoration; it does not delete items from the current table based on their expiration times.

choices.text: Change the table class to Standard-IA to handle item expiration.
choices.explanation: This changes storage and access rates, but does not configure per-item expiration or deletion.

source.label: Amazon DynamoDB — Time to Live

learning.reason: Manage expiration with a TTL attribute and exclude expired items from reads until they are deleted. Background deletion avoids having to run large-scale deletion jobs yourself.
learning.concept: DynamoDB TTL does not guarantee deletion at an exact time. The application's read path must enforce the display deadline.

title: Include department tags in billing data aggregation
prompt: Multiple teams share member accounts in the same AWS Organizations organization. Each resource for a service subject to cost allocation already has a user-defined tag indicating its department. You want to group future charges by department in the management account's Cost Explorer, but the tag you created is not yet available as a grouping option. What setting should you configure next?

choices.text: Change the tag values to member account names so that departments within the same account are separated automatically.
choices.explanation: Replacing the values with account names would not distinguish departments within the same account, and it would not activate the cost allocation tag.

choices.text: Apply only a tag policy and assume that compliant tag values will automatically appear in billing aggregation.
choices.explanation: Tag policies manage naming conventions. The tag key must be activated separately for billing.

choices.text: Select linked accounts in Cost Explorer and group by account only.
choices.explanation: Departments sharing the same member account cannot be distinguished at the account level.

choices.text: In billing management for the management account, activate the tag key as a user-defined cost allocation tag.
choices.explanation: This makes it possible to group the corresponding costs by department tag value.

source.label: AWS Billing — ユーザー定義のコスト配分タグ

learning.reason: Activate the tag key as a cost allocation tag in billing management for the management account. It may take time for the tag to appear.
learning.concept: Tagging a resource with a value and enabling that tag key for cost aggregation are separate operations.

sourceLabel: AWS Billing — User-defined cost allocation tags

title: Store rarely used annual EBS snapshots at lower cost
prompt: The application can be restored quickly from recent EBS snapshots. Annual snapshots created separately for audit purposes must be retained for at least one year, and taking up to 72 hours to restore an archive is acceptable. Cost estimates show that archiving the annual snapshots at full size still reduces storage costs. How should you preserve the daily restore procedure and design the restore procedure for the annual snapshots?

choices.text: Move only the annual snapshots to Snapshot Archive, and restore them to Standard before creating a volume when needed.
choices.explanation: This keeps recent snapshots available for quick restores while allowing lower-cost long-term storage and restore delays for the annual snapshots.

choices.text: Archive both recent and annual snapshots, then create new EBS volumes directly from the archive when needed.
choices.explanation: You cannot create a volume directly before restoring the snapshot to Standard, and this does not meet the requirement for quick restores from recent snapshots.

choices.text: Keep the annual snapshots in their current storage tier and assume that enabling Fast Snapshot Restore will reduce storage charges.
choices.explanation: This setting speeds up volume initialization after a restore; it does not move snapshots to a lower-cost storage tier.

choices.text: Keep the annual snapshots in Standard and change only the copied EBS volumes to a lower-cost volume type.
choices.explanation: Changing a volume type does not change the storage tier of snapshots you already retain.

source.label: Amazon EBS — スナップショットアーカイブ

learning.reason: Move only the annual snapshots to the archive. When one is needed, restore it to the Standard tier before creating a volume from it.
learning.concept: Snapshot Archive is intended for long-term retention, and archiving converts a snapshot to a full snapshot. You cannot create a volume while the snapshot remains archived.

title: Speed up a product page that reads the same DynamoDB items
prompt: During a sale, the DynamoDB product table receives repeated GetItem requests for a small set of the same product IDs. The results can be briefly stale, and the goal is submillisecond reads when the cache has a hit. You want to use DynamoDB-compatible reads without managing a separate cache data model or invalidation logic in Lambda. What should you choose?

choices.text: Increase DynamoDB read capacity and make all reads strongly consistent.
choices.explanation: This may address throttling, but it does not reuse the target items in memory.

choices.text: Add DAX, use a compatible client, and cache repeated eventually consistent reads.
choices.explanation: A cache hit can speed up frequent reads of the same items.

choices.text: Design separate keys in ElastiCache and implement cache population and expiration in Lambda.
choices.explanation: This can provide fast reads, but you must operate a separate data model and cache logic yourself.

choices.text: Use DynamoDB global tables from the same Region to cache reads of the same items.
choices.explanation: Global tables replicate data between Regions; they do not add an in-memory cache for the requester.

source.label: Amazon DynamoDB — DynamoDB Accelerator

learning.reason: With a DAX cluster and a compatible client, cache hits for eventually consistent reads can provide low latency.
learning.concept: DAX is an in-memory cache integrated with DynamoDB. Requests that do not use the cache, such as strongly consistent reads, are passed through to DynamoDB.

title: Limit Lambda concurrency for only one SQS queue
prompt: Lambda receives messages through on-demand polling from a standard SQS queue, and another application invokes the function directly. When the SQS queue is busy, connections from Lambda to the database spike. Without stopping message reception or imposing a new concurrency limit on direct invocations of the same Lambda function, you want to limit concurrent processing through SQS to a specified number. Which setting is appropriate?

choices.text: Change only the Lambda function's reserved concurrency to the number of executions the SQS queue can support.
choices.explanation: This limits the function's overall concurrency, so direct invocations are constrained too.

choices.text: Change only the SQS batch size and assume it sets a new fixed limit on the number of batches running concurrently.
choices.explanation: Batch size is the number of messages passed in one invocation; it does not cap concurrent invocations.

choices.text: Shorten the SQS visibility timeout to impose a uniform limit on new Lambda invocations.
choices.explanation: This changes when a message can be received again; it does not set a limit on the number of Lambda invocations.

choices.text: Set maximum concurrency in the event source mapping for the target SQS queue, and ensure that sufficient function and account concurrency capacity is available.
choices.explanation: This limits executions through the queue; the setting itself does not apply to direct invocations.

source.label: AWS Lambda — SQSのイベントソースマッピングのスケーリング

learning.reason: Set maximum concurrency in the SQS event source mapping to limit invocations from the target queue.
learning.concept: Reserved concurrency applies to the entire function. Maximum concurrency on a standard SQS event source mapping applies per event source.

sourceLabel: AWS Lambda — SQS event source mapping scaling

title: Skip registration for regularly added Athena partitions
prompt: Daily logs in S3 are stored under regular year, month, and day paths, and the data for each required day exists. Athena queries always specify a condition on the day. To reduce query-planning and daily metadata-registration overhead, you want Athena to calculate the S3 location from the date. Keep the file format and paths unchanged. What should you configure?

choices.text: Run MSCK REPAIR TABLE daily to add new partitions to the Glue Data Catalog.
choices.explanation: This can be automated, but it does not meet the requirement to avoid daily registration and retrieving partitions from the catalog.

choices.text: Create only a Glue partition index and assume the index automatically registers new partitions.
choices.explanation: An index improves searches for registered partitions; it does not calculate new locations from date rules.

choices.text: Enable date-based partition projection in Athena, configure it to match the existing paths, and filter by date.
choices.explanation: Athena can calculate the S3 paths needed for a query without a registration job.

choices.text: Remove the date condition from SQL and rely on the Athena query result cache to discover new daily partitions.
choices.explanation: The result cache does not generate metadata. New data must still be discovered, and date ranges must still be handled.

source.label: Amazon Athena — パーティション射影

learning.reason: Configure the date type and range in partition projection, and define the S3 location pattern that matches the paths.
learning.concept: Partition projection calculates partitions from rules, so you do not have to retrieve each registered date value from the catalog for every query.

title: Reduce TCP tail latency with the existing EC2 placement
prompt: Long-lived TCP streams run between supported EC2 instances in the same subnet. Average latency is acceptable, but the 99th percentile rises under congestion. The current instance types, placement, and application TCP protocol must remain unchanged, and both ends use supported versions of the network driver. Which feature should be enabled at both ends?

choices.text: Enable ENA Express on the network interfaces at both ends.
choices.explanation: It uses SRD for supported flows, helping reduce tail latency during congestion.

choices.text: Move the EC2 instances to a different cluster placement group.
choices.explanation: This can improve proximity, but it does not meet the requirement to preserve the existing placement and improve supported flows.

choices.text: Change the application to use a high-performance communication library that supports EFA OS bypass.
choices.explanation: This can help with high-performance computing, but it violates the requirement to keep the existing application's TCP communication unchanged.

choices.text: Relay the TCP traffic between the two instances through a public Global Accelerator endpoint, including traffic within the same subnet.
choices.explanation: Global Accelerator provides an entry point for distributed clients. It is not a way to improve direct communication within the same subnet.

source.label: Amazon EC2 — ENA Express

learning.reason: Enable ENA Express on the supported network interfaces. SRD can be used for supported TCP communication when both ends are configured for it.
learning.concept: ENA Express handles communication between supported EC2 instances; it is different from placing instances closer together or changing TCP to MPI.

title: Remove the EC2 bandwidth limit on EBS volumes with spare capacity
prompt: A database on a single EC2 instance reads from multiple EBS volumes at the same time. The volumes have spare IOPS and throughput, but the instance's aggregate EBS bandwidth has reached its limit. Additional EBS bandwidth cannot be configured for this instance, and splitting the database is not allowed. Which change increases aggregate bandwidth while keeping the database and volumes?

choices.text: Increase the provisioned IOPS and throughput for every volume, and keep the instance.
choices.explanation: The volumes already have spare capacity. This does not raise the instance's aggregate bandwidth limit.

choices.text: Add more volumes to further distribute the database storage, and attach them to the same EC2 instance.
choices.explanation: As long as the volumes are attached to the same instance, aggregate bandwidth remains constrained by the instance limit.

choices.text: Switch to a compatible instance type with higher sustained EBS bandwidth, and use the existing volumes.
choices.explanation: This raises the instance limit that was constraining the available bandwidth from the volumes.

choices.text: Choose an instance type with higher internet transfer performance only, without comparing EBS-optimized bandwidth.
choices.explanation: Higher network bandwidth for internet traffic does not necessarily meet the requirement for dedicated EBS bandwidth.

source.label: Amazon EC2 — EBS最適化インスタンスタイプ

learning.reason: Choose an instance type that supports the existing volumes and provides higher sustained EBS-optimized bandwidth.
learning.concept: EBS data transfer is constrained by both volume performance and the instance's aggregate limit. Increasing only the side with spare capacity does not remove the bottleneck.

title: Shorten the queue for Redshift dashboard queries
prompt: A provisioned Redshift cluster uses a dedicated WLM queue for dashboard reads. Individual queries run quickly enough, but their wait time grows when access surges. The queries and tables cannot be changed, and you do not want to keep extra nodes running during normal periods. The queries support concurrency scaling. What should you configure?

choices.text: Run VACUUM on the tables regularly to clear the queue with the same execution capacity.
choices.explanation: Table maintenance can improve scan performance, but it does not add compute resources to run queries concurrently as demand increases.

choices.text: Pin all dashboard queries to one WLM slot.
choices.explanation: This further limits the number of queries that can run concurrently and does not improve the wait time.

choices.text: Enable concurrency scaling for the target WLM queue.
choices.explanation: This adds execution capacity for supported queries during surges, without permanently adding nodes to the base cluster just for peak demand.

choices.text: Only raise the dashboard queue's priority and assume that external concurrency capacity will also be added when needed.
choices.explanation: Priority affects how available capacity is allocated. Changing priority alone does not enable additional clusters.

source.label: Amazon Redshift — 同時実行スケーリング

learning.reason: Enabling concurrency scaling for the target WLM queue makes additional execution infrastructure available when demand rises.
learning.concept: Even an efficient query plan can face long waits when there is not enough capacity to run queries concurrently. Additional capacity can reduce those waits.

title: Distribute large scans from Aurora MySQL to the storage layer
prompt: An Aurora MySQL cluster with a supported version and instance type runs an analytical query that scans many pages and filters out most of them with a WHERE condition. The query is eligible for this optimization, and the current issue is not the number of connections or concurrent queries. Which feature reduces the intermediate data sent from storage to DB nodes without moving the data to another service?

choices.text: Enable Aurora MySQL parallel query so the target query can use row retrieval and filtering in the storage layer.
choices.explanation: It can distribute the applicable scan and filtering work, reducing the intermediate data handled by DB nodes.

choices.text: Run the same query concurrently on multiple Aurora Replicas, then use the single result that finishes last.
choices.explanation: Replicas can add read targets, but this does not push an individual scan down to distributed storage.

choices.text: Add RDS Proxy and assign multiple pooled connections to the target query.
choices.explanation: A proxy manages database connections; it does not change the storage execution plan for a single SQL statement.

choices.text: Add Aurora write targets across Regions and run the analytical query on the current cluster.
choices.explanation: The write-side configuration does not push the target read processing down to storage.

source.label: Amazon Aurora — Aurora MySQLのパラレルクエリ

learning.reason: Aurora parallel query moves some row retrieval and filtering for supported large queries to distributed storage nodes.
learning.concept: Running a query concurrently on multiple instances is different from pushing the data processing for one query down to the storage layer.

sourceLabel: Amazon Aurora — Aurora MySQL parallel query

title: Speed up first reads immediately after restoring from EBS
prompt: During monthly recovery drills, you create a volume in a specific AZ from an existing EBS snapshot. The volume's size and IOPS meet the requirements, but only the first access to blocks that have not yet been read is slow. You want the volume to deliver performance from the start of the drill without manually reading every block after creation. You can complete the configuration in advance and reserve the required volume creation quota. What should you choose?

choices.text: Create a volume from the snapshot with only its gp3 IOPS increased.
choices.explanation: This raises the configured performance for normal blocks but does not address initialization on their first read.

choices.text: Enable Fast Snapshot Restore in advance for the snapshot in the AZ where recovery will take place.
choices.explanation: Under the applicable conditions, a volume created in that AZ can deliver full performance from the time it is created.

choices.text: Copy the snapshot to another snapshot in the Standard storage tier, then restore from that copy.
choices.explanation: Creating another copy does not by itself guarantee initialization of every block on the volume.

choices.text: Enable Fast Snapshot Restore only in an AZ other than the target AZ, then create the volume in the target AZ.
choices.explanation: The setting applies to a specific snapshot and AZ combination, so it does not apply to a different AZ.

source.label: Amazon EBS — Fast Snapshot Restore

learning.reason: Enable Fast Snapshot Restore for the specified snapshot and AZ. After it is enabled, you can use volumes created there in an initialized state.
learning.concept: Fast Snapshot Restore is configured for a snapshot and AZ combination. A method that speeds up volume creation or lowers snapshot storage costs is not a substitute by itself.

title: Scale on ALB requests when CPU usage misses congestion
prompt: An ECS service using the standard rolling deployment strategy processes HTTP requests through an ALB target group. The service spends a long time waiting for an external API, so CPU utilization stays low even as load increases. However, the request count per healthy target is strongly correlated with latency. Which setting scales the number of tasks up or down toward a constant workload per target, without manually tuning thresholds?

choices.text: Set a target for the service's average CPU utilization and add tasks only when CPU exceeds the threshold.
choices.explanation: Here, external wait time dominates, so CPU utilization is unlikely to capture request congestion.

choices.text: Use the total number of ALB requests and add tasks to maintain a constant total.
choices.explanation: Adding tasks does not reduce the total number of requests from users. The target must be a per-target workload.

choices.text: Change the ECS deployment minimum healthy percentage and rely on that percentage to scale with normal traffic.
choices.explanation: This setting controls the number of tasks maintained during a deployment; it does not track request load during normal operation.

choices.text: Create a target tracking policy using ALBRequestCountPerTarget for the target group.
choices.explanation: This metric represents the average workload on healthy targets and can be used to adjust the service's task count.

source.label: Amazon ECS — ターゲット追跡スケーリング

learning.reason: In ECS Service Auto Scaling, specify ALBRequestCountPerTarget for the target group and set a workload target.
learning.concept: With target tracking, choose a metric that changes as capacity is added or removed. The total request count alone will not fall when you add tasks.

title: Observe a 20% AMI refresh for a set period, then resume
prompt: You are updating the AMI for an EC2 Auto Scaling group with an instance refresh. When 20% of the instances have been replaced, notify the operations team so it can observe the error rate for 15 minutes. If an issue is detected, cancel the refresh; otherwise, continue with the remaining instances without an approval action. Which settings are appropriate?

choices.text: Set a 15-minute warmup for each instance and expect the refresh to stop when 20% of the fleet has been replaced.
choices.explanation: Warmup is a wait period for each new instance, not a checkpoint based on the overall replacement percentage.

choices.text: Lower the minimum healthy percentage to 20% and reduce the desired capacity to 20% only during the observation period.
choices.explanation: This setting defines the minimum healthy capacity. It is unnecessary to reduce desired capacity, and it does not provide a progress notification followed by a fixed pause.

choices.text: Set 20% and 100% as the instance refresh checkpoints, set the checkpoint delay to 15 minutes, and notify on reaching a checkpoint.
choices.explanation: This allows time to inspect the refresh at 20%, cancel it if an issue is found, and continue automatically after the delay.

choices.text: Update only the AMI in the launch template and let the tasks determine whether a checkpoint is needed.
choices.explanation: Changing the AMI alone does not configure a staged replacement of existing instances or an observation period.

source.label: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling — インスタンスリフレッシュのチェックポイント

learning.reason: Set a checkpoint at 20% and the final replacement percentage at 100%. Set the checkpoint delay to 15 minutes. Notify on checkpoint arrival and cancel the refresh before it continues if an issue is found.
learning.concept: A checkpoint pauses the overall replacement progress for a set period. When the delay expires, the refresh proceeds automatically to the next stage.

sourceLabel: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling — Instance refresh checkpoints

title: Resume TTL processing and change notifications on a point-in-time restored DynamoDB table
prompt: To recover from an erroneous update, you used point-in-time recovery (PITR) to restore a DynamoDB table fully to a new table in the same Region before the update. No settings were excluded during the restore, and validation confirmed the data and existing secondary indexes. After cutover, automatic deletion based on an expiration attribute and downstream processing of changes must continue. The connection destination and permissions have been updated, and the Lambda change-notification destination will be updated separately. Select two settings required on the new table before cutover.

choices.text: Enable TTL on the restored table, specifying the same attribute as the original table.
choices.explanation: Expiration values are restored as data, but the table setting that applies TTL is not restored automatically.

choices.text: Recreate the original table's partition key on the restored table after the restore completes.
choices.explanation: The restored table already has the corresponding key schema. Recreating it does not enable TTL or streams.

choices.text: Delete the validated global secondary index and recreate it with the same definition.
choices.explanation: The index was not excluded and its presence was confirmed. Recreating it does not enable notifications or expiration processing.

choices.text: Re-enable streams on the original table and assume changes to the restored table will be added there automatically.
choices.explanation: Stream records are created per table. The original table's stream does not record changes to the restored table.

choices.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams on the restored table with the required view type.
choices.explanation: The restored table's stream settings are not carried over, so you must configure them to send changes from the cutover table downstream.

source.label: Amazon DynamoDB — テーブルの復元と再設定

learning.reason: Attributes retained on the restored table can be used as they are, but TTL and DynamoDB Streams must be configured again on the restored table.
learning.concept: Point-in-time recovery restores data and corresponding settings to a new table. Some features, such as TTL and streams, require configuration after the restore.

sourceLabel: Amazon DynamoDB — Table restore and reconfiguration

title: Extend the visibility timeout for SQS messages under prolonged review
prompt: Normal processing of a standard SQS queue finishes within 2 minutes, but an external review can continue for 15 minutes. Each worker can check progress while a task is running, and processing is idempotent. Which approach should be used to suppress redelivery caused by the visibility timeout only for long-running tasks that are progressing normally, without increasing the failure wait time for every message?

choices.text: Increase the default visibility timeout for all messages so that retries for short tasks also wait for the same longer period.
choices.explanation: This may accommodate long-running tasks, but it does not meet the requirement to avoid delaying redelivery of short tasks after a failure.

choices.text: Keep the normal visibility timeout, and extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility before it expires only for messages being processed. Delete each message after processing completes.
choices.explanation: This prevents a normally progressing long-running task from becoming visible again. If a worker stops, the message can be retried after the timeout expires.

choices.text: Delete a message from the queue as soon as it is sent for external review, then retry using the original SQS message even if the review result is lost.
choices.explanation: A deleted message cannot be redelivered if processing fails partway through.

choices.text: Extend only the queue's retention period.
choices.explanation: The retention period for an undeleted message and the time before a received message becomes visible again are configured separately.

source.label: Amazon SQS — 可視性タイムアウト

learning.reason: Keep the normal visibility timeout for short tasks and extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility only for messages whose processing is continuing.
learning.concept: Visibility suppresses normal redelivery to other workers after a message is received. A standard queue provides at-least-once delivery, so processing must remain idempotent alongside visibility extensions.

title: Perform point-in-time recovery in another Region without a running standby database
prompt: A Multi-AZ DB instance for RDS for PostgreSQL is in use. For disaster recovery in another Region, you do not want to keep a replica running, and you want to be able to choose a recovery time from the recoverable time range already transferred to the destination, including times other than the daily snapshot times. The engine and Region combination is supported. Which approach is appropriate?

choices.text: Copy only manually created daily snapshots to another Region.
choices.explanation: You can restore to the time captured by a snapshot stored in the destination, but no logs are replicated to support recovery to an intervening time.

choices.text: Keep a read replica in another Region and promote it during a failure.
choices.explanation: This can be a recovery approach, but it conflicts with the requirement not to keep a replica running. The replica's state is not a backup for an arbitrary point in time.

choices.text: Replicate the DB instance's automated backups to another Region. During a disaster, perform a point-in-time recovery in the destination from the time range available there to create a new DB instance.
choices.explanation: The destination can use transaction logs, allowing recovery to a time other than a daily snapshot time.

choices.text: Take automated backups in the same Region, then rely on backups in the source Region from the destination Region's point-in-time recovery target.
choices.explanation: Without automated backups and logs available in the destination, this does not provide independent point-in-time recovery for an outage in the source Region.

source.label: Amazon RDS — 自動バックアップのクロスリージョン複製

learning.reason: RDS automated backup replication sends snapshots and transaction logs to the destination Region. A DB can be restored to a specified point in the transferred time range.
learning.concept: Copying daily snapshots preserves snapshot recovery points. Point-in-time recovery also uses transaction logs created after a snapshot.
