learning.concept: SAML federation is used for sign-in, while SCIM provisions external IdP users and groups. Permission sets manage account access.

sourceLabel: AWS IAM Identity Center — automatic provisioning from an external IdP

title: Validate client certificates from an internal CA with an ALB
prompt: An ALB for a B2B API already has a server certificate configured. Corporate clients connecting to it must also present certificates issued by a CA trusted by the organization, and the certificates must be validated for trust at the ALB before requests reach the application. The application cannot be modified to validate certificate chains. Which configuration should you use?

choices.text: Use mTLS passthrough on the HTTPS listener and validate the presented certificate chain in the backend.
choices.explanation: This performs validation in the application and does not meet the requirement for the ALB to validate the certificate.

choices.text: Enable mTLS in verify mode and associate a trust store containing the internal CA with the HTTPS listener.
choices.explanation: The ALB can validate the client certificate.

choices.text: Add another server certificate to ACM and treat it as validation of client certificates on the same listener.
choices.explanation: An additional server certificate is used by the ALB to authenticate itself to clients. It is not a trust store for client authentication.

choices.text: Allow the clients' source IP addresses in the security group and use that instead of certificate validation.
choices.explanation: This restricts network sources but does not validate certificates presented by clients.

source.label: Elastic Load Balancing — ALBの相互TLS

learning.reason: Enable mTLS verify mode on the HTTPS listener and associate a trust store containing the trusted CA. The ALB can then validate client certificates.
learning.concept: The server certificate identifies the ALB to clients. In mutual TLS verify mode, the ALB also validates client certificates.

sourceLabel: Elastic Load Balancing — ALB mutual TLS

title: Use a specified key for S3 writes without encryption headers
prompt: Only an application with the KMS permissions required for Amazon S3 writes new data to a dedicated S3 general purpose bucket. The existing application uses PutObject without specifying an encryption method. Which setting should you use to make these writes use a particular customer managed KMS key without changing the code?

choices.text: Set the bucket's default to SSE-S3 and add only permissions for the application to access the KMS key.
choices.explanation: SSE-S3 uses keys managed by Amazon S3. Giving the application permission to use a KMS key does not change the encryption key to that specified KMS key.

choices.text: Reject PutObject when the encryption header containing the specified KMS key is omitted.
choices.explanation: The application would no longer be able to write, so this does not meet the requirement to leave its code unchanged.

choices.text: Copy existing objects with encryption enabled and assume that future PutObject requests will use the same key without changing the default encryption.
choices.explanation: This can encrypt the objects that are copied, but it does not change the default for other objects written later.

choices.text: Configure the bucket's default encryption to use SSE-KMS with the specified customer managed key.
choices.explanation: This applies the desired encryption method and key to new writes for which the application does not specify encryption.

source.label: Amazon S3 — バケットの既定暗号化

learning.reason: Set the bucket's default encryption to SSE-KMS and specify the KMS key to use. This setting applies when the application omits an encryption method.
learning.concept: Default encryption sets the default for newly stored data. Separate access controls are needed if you want to restrict explicit client-side encryption choices.

title: Allow an analytics application to use only an S3 access point with a VPC origin
prompt: An analytics application needs to read a specific prefix from an existing S3 general purpose bucket. The bucket policy denies direct access and can delegate access to this application's access point. The access point must also be reachable only from a specified VPC, and the endpoint in use is already configured. How should you configure it?

choices.text: Set the access point's network origin to the specified VPC and grant the analytics role access only to the required prefix.
choices.explanation: This limits the network origin to the specified VPC and scopes access to the role and data prefix.

choices.text: Set the network origin to the internet and specify only the role and prefix.
choices.explanation: This limits the identity and data scope, but does not prevent the same role from being used outside the VPC.

choices.text: Remove the existing setting that denies direct bucket access and connect directly to the bucket's public endpoint from the VPC.
choices.explanation: This violates the requirement to allow access only through the access point.

choices.text: Keep the access point's internet origin and record the application's deployment subnet name in a tag.
choices.explanation: A tag does not change the access point's network origin to a VPC.

source.label: Amazon S3 — VPCに制限したアクセスポイント

learning.reason: Set the access point's network origin to the specified VPC and use its policy to grant access to the role and prefix.
learning.concept: Bucket delegation and access point permissions work together. A VPC origin restricts the network from which requests can reach the access point.

sourceLabel: Amazon S3 — access points restricted to a VPC

title: Separate the permissions needed to start scheduled ECS tasks
prompt: An EventBridge rule calls ECS RunTask. The application's task role and the ECS task execution role are specified, but the EventBridge target IAM role has only ecs:RunTask for the task definition. The task failed to start because the target role lacked permission to pass these roles. Which permissions should you configure?

choices.text: Allow the application's task role to assume the EventBridge target role.
choices.explanation: The application task has not started yet. The principal requesting RunTask needs the required permissions.

choices.text: Grant ecs:RunTask to the task execution role and leave the target role's current permissions unchanged.
choices.explanation: The EventBridge role that requests the task still lacks permission to pass the other roles.

choices.text: Add iam:PassRole to the EventBridge target role for only the specified task role and task execution role.
choices.explanation: The target role can pass both authorized roles to ECS and start the task.

choices.text: Add only iam:ListRoles to the EventBridge target role so it can retrieve the role names before starting the task.
choices.explanation: Permission to list roles does not grant permission to pass them to ECS.

source.label: Amazon ECS — EventBridgeのIAMロール

learning.reason: Allow iam:PassRole on the specified task role and task execution role for the EventBridge target role.
learning.concept: The EventBridge target role calls AWS APIs. When a task starts with other IAM roles, the caller needs PassRole permission scoped to those roles.

title: Direct Client VPN destinations by department
prompt: Client VPN users authenticated through the same Active Directory belong to development and operations groups. Routes to both corresponding subnets are already in place. Configure the VPN endpoint so that development users can send traffic only to development destinations, and operations users only to operations destinations. Which configuration should you add?

choices.text: Rely only on directory authentication and grant every user authorization to all destinations.
choices.explanation: Being authenticated as a user and being authorized to reach a specific destination are separate controls.

choices.text: Create Client VPN authorization rules for each destination CIDR and specify the corresponding directory group in each rule.
choices.explanation: This restricts destinations by group while using the same VPN connection and existing routes.

choices.text: Specify the development and operations AD group names as sources in network ACLs for the VPN subnets.
choices.explanation: Network ACLs cannot directly specify directory group names.

choices.text: Record group names in VPN connection logs and leave route authorization open to all users.
choices.explanation: Logs can support investigation, but they do not authorize connection requests by group.

source.label: AWS Client VPN — 認可ルール

learning.reason: Use Client VPN authorization rules to specify which directory group is allowed for each destination CIDR.
learning.concept: VPN routes provide a path to destinations. Authorization rules control which user groups may access each destination CIDR.

title: Classify allowed automated access and unwanted access
prompt: A public website uses AWS WAF, and simple per-IP rate limiting cannot distinguish high volumes of legitimate search engine traffic from other automated access. You need to investigate known bots in the logs by managed category and verification status, then add protective rules using that information. Do not modify the application. What should you use?

choices.text: Use a single per-IP rate-based rule for all requests and assume it can distinguish traffic at the same rate by category.
choices.explanation: Per-source frequency can be measured, but this does not provide managed bot categories or verification information.

choices.text: Use only the existing generic input inspection rules and treat SQL injection results as a bot's verification status.
choices.explanation: Inspecting malicious input cannot determine whether a request came from a verified bot.

choices.text: Add the AWS WAF Bot Control managed rule group to the web ACL and design rule actions based on its classifications.
choices.explanation: You can inspect the detected categories and verification labels, then distinguish how legitimate automated traffic is handled.

choices.text: Only extend WAF log retention and assume that managed bot classification will be performed.
choices.explanation: Log retention changes how long collected records are stored; it does not add classification to requests.

source.label: AWS WAF — Bot Control管理ルールグループ

learning.reason: Use classifications and labels from the Bot Control managed rule group to choose actions based on the category and verification status.
learning.concept: Per-IP rate limiting measures frequency. Bot Control uses managed classifications and verification information for investigation and policy enforcement.

sourceLabel: AWS WAF — Bot Control managed rule group

title: Fargate without an internet route uses private ECR
prompt: Launch a task on the standard Fargate platform version 1.4.0 or later in a private subnet with no internet route. The image is already stored in private ECR in the same Region, and pull-through cache is not used. Permissions for the task execution role are configured. Select two connections needed to retrieve the image.

choices.text: Configure only ecr.dkr and assume that a route to the ECR API is unnecessary on version 1.4.0 or later.
choices.explanation: Both the ECR API endpoint and the Docker endpoint are required for the platform versions in scope.

choices.text: Create interface endpoints for ecr.api and ecr.dkr, and make them available to tasks through DNS and security groups.
choices.explanation: This provides access to the ECR API and private registry without going through the internet.

choices.text: Create only an ECS control plane endpoint and retrieve image layers through it.
choices.explanation: A route to the ECS management API does not replace connectivity to ECR and S3.

choices.text: Create the required S3 gateway endpoint and associate it with the route table used by the tasks.
choices.explanation: This provides internet-free access to S3, where image layers are stored.

choices.text: Use a CloudWatch Logs interface endpoint to forward ECR and S3 requests through it.
choices.explanation: A logging endpoint cannot retrieve images from ECR and S3.

source.label: Amazon ECR — インターフェイスVPCエンドポイント

learning.reason: Provide interface endpoints for the ECR API and Docker registry, along with an endpoint for S3 to retrieve image layers.
learning.concept: Retrieving a private image involves connecting to ECR for authorization and registry access, and to S3 for the image layers.

title: Block a broadly shared secret policy before it is applied
prompt: An operations pipeline applies a resource policy to each secret in Secrets Manager, specifying approved roles. You need to stop an erroneous policy from being submitted when it would expose access broadly, rather than wait to detect it later. Keep the current KMS key and valid individual policies. Which setting should the pipeline use?

choices.text: Enable BlockPublicPolicy in the PutResourcePolicy call.
choices.explanation: Secrets Manager evaluates the policy and does not apply one that grants broad access.

choices.text: Apply the resource policy as is, then search CloudTrail the next day for broad permissions.
choices.explanation: This supports later investigation but does not stop a policy that mistakenly grants broad access before it is applied.

choices.text: Only shorten the secret rotation interval.
choices.explanation: Changing the secret value does not evaluate who is authorized to retrieve the current value.

choices.text: Associate the same policy with an AWS managed key and assume that the key will automatically validate the secret's policy.
choices.explanation: KMS encryption and pre-application validation of a Secrets Manager resource policy are separate controls.

source.label: AWS Secrets Manager — リソースベースのポリシー検証

learning.reason: Enable BlockPublicPolicy in PutResourcePolicy to prevent a resource policy that grants broad access from being attached.
learning.concept: Secrets Manager can evaluate a secret's resource policy. Auditing a stored policy alone cannot prevent it before application.

sourceLabel: AWS Secrets Manager — Resource-based policy validation

title: Restore a KMS key to its original use before deletion
prompt: A customer managed KMS key used by a production application was accidentally scheduled for deletion. The waiting period has not ended, and the ciphertext was created with this key. How can you resume decryption with the original key without re-encrypting the existing data?

choices.text: Cancel the scheduled deletion and assume the key is immediately Enabled and ready to use.
choices.explanation: A key whose deletion has been canceled is Disabled. It must also be enabled before use can resume.

choices.text: Keep the deletion scheduled, create a new key with the same alias, and use it to decrypt the existing ciphertext.
choices.explanation: A different key does not have the same key material. Giving it the same alias does not let it decrypt ciphertext created with the original key.

choices.text: Wait until the waiting period ends, then restore the fully deleted key with the same key ID.
choices.explanation: A deleted KMS key cannot be restored this way. You must act during the waiting period.

choices.text: Cancel the scheduled deletion, then enable the original key, which is Disabled.
choices.explanation: You can reuse the same key and decrypt data that was encrypted with it.

source.label: AWS KMS — キーの削除予定の取り消し

learning.reason: Canceling the scheduled deletion moves the key to Disabled. Enable that same key to resume using it.
learning.concept: You can cancel a scheduled deletion during the waiting period. Canceling it does not automatically make the key ready for encryption and decryption again.

title: Check how much of a purchased Savings Plan was used
prompt: Some workloads have been retired, and the commitment for an already purchased Compute Savings Plan may not be fully used. For the current agreement, you want to find the commitment used and unused during a specific period. Which report should you use?

choices.text: Review only the Savings Plans coverage report.
choices.explanation: It shows how much of the eligible usage was covered by a discount. It is not the report for finding the unused amount of a purchase.

choices.text: Use the Savings Plans utilization report, filtered by period and purchased plan.
choices.explanation: It shows the commitment used and the unused portion.

choices.text: Review only the Savings Plans purchase recommendations.
choices.explanation: These help you consider future purchases and do not directly show the performance of an existing agreement.

choices.text: Review only the forecast cost in AWS Budgets.
choices.explanation: This is a billing forecast, not a way to see the unused portion of a specific agreement.

source.label: AWS Savings Plans — 使用率レポート

learning.reason: Use the Savings Plans utilization report to see how much of a purchased commitment was used.
learning.concept: Utilization uses the commitment as its basis, while coverage uses eligible usage. Both relate to discounts, but they measure different things.

title: Break down a shared account’s bill to individual resources
prompt: A finance analyst uses SQL to aggregate, day by day from S3, the charges for services that provide resource IDs in a shared AWS account used by several teams. The current CUR 2.0 report contains only service-level aggregates. Without changing service usage, the analyst wants to associate supported usage line items with individual IDs, such as EC2 resource IDs, going forward. What should be configured?

choices.text: Enable only cost allocation tags and assume individual AWS resource IDs will automatically appear in the service-level aggregates.
choices.explanation: Tags can identify teams, but this does not configure the export to provide usage details at the resource level.

choices.text: Change CUR 2.0 to monthly and export the same service-level columns as before.
choices.explanation: Changing the reporting period does not add resource IDs to usage line items.

choices.text: Add service aggregates to AWS Budgets actual-cost notifications and infer resource IDs with SQL.
choices.explanation: Service-level aggregates cannot identify the AWS resource whose usage generated a charge.

choices.text: Enable INCLUDE_RESOURCES in CUR 2.0 and export usage line items and line_item_resource_id to S3.
choices.explanation: This provides resource IDs directly for supported usage, so SQL can aggregate costs for individual resources.

source.label: AWS Data Exports — CUR 2.0

learning.reason: Enable INCLUDE_RESOURCES in CUR 2.0 to include the resource ID column in the export.
learning.concept: Selecting resource-level granularity exports supported usage line items by resource. The export can be larger than one containing only aggregates.

title: Avoid adding EBS for a rebuildable batch workspace
prompt: An EC2 batch job reads source files from S3, transforms them in a workspace, and writes the results to S3. The instance type in use has enough instance store capacity. If unfinished temporary data is lost when the host is replaced, the job can be rerun from the source files, and the temporary data does not need to be retained after the job completes. Where should the job store its temporary data without using an additional persistent volume?

choices.text: Use the instance store as the workspace and continue saving the results to S3.
choices.explanation: If the temporary workspace is lost, it can be rebuilt from the S3 source files, so no additional EBS volume is needed for the job.

choices.text: Attach a new EBS volume for each job and detach it before the job ends.
choices.explanation: This provides a separate workspace, but uses an additional persistent volume for every job.

choices.text: Write temporary files directly to an on-demand EBS snapshot.
choices.explanation: A snapshot is not a workspace block device that can be mounted directly.

choices.text: Create a new EFS file system shared across Availability Zones and store all temporary data there.
choices.explanation: This adds shared, persistent storage instead of using the available workspace on the host.

source.label: Amazon EC2 — インスタンスストア

learning.reason: Use the available instance store for temporary data, while continuing to keep the source files and results in S3.
learning.concept: Instance store is temporary block storage attached to a host. Do not use it for data that must be retained across a stop or termination.

title: Avoid rescanning data for repeated Athena queries
prompt: The same SQL query is submitted every few minutes from the same Athena workgroup against finalized data. The query and result location are unchanged, and results may be up to 15 minutes old. Without introducing a precomputed table or an external cache, how can you avoid rescanning the source data when the same result already exists?

choices.text: Set only a scanned-bytes limit for the workgroup.
choices.explanation: This can cap costs, but it does not automatically reuse a previous result for the same query.

choices.text: Convert the S3 objects to Parquet and run the same SQL query for every request.
choices.explanation: This can reduce the amount read per run, but the source data is still rescanned even when a previous result exists.

choices.text: Enable query result reuse in the same workgroup and set the maximum age to 15 minutes.
choices.explanation: If a matching result exists within the time limit, Athena can skip executing the original query.

choices.text: Share only the output S3 bucket and send each request to a different workgroup.
choices.explanation: Using the same output location alone does not allow Athena to reuse results across workgroups.

source.label: Amazon Athena — クエリ結果の再利用

learning.reason: Enable Athena query result reuse and set the maximum result age to 15 minutes.
learning.concept: When a matching result within the age limit exists in the same workgroup, Athena can skip running the query. A short validity period and finalized data help control the freshness of results.

title: Use shared RDS Proxy connections with one-time common initialization
prompt: Connections to RDS for MySQL already go through RDS Proxy. Profiling shows that every client sends the same set of multiple SET statements each time it obtains a connection, and a particular setting causes connection pinning. Every client needs the selected setting values, which differ from the backend connections' defaults. The application clients can be changed. How can you preserve this initialization while maintaining connection multiplexing?

choices.text: Register the common SET statements as initialization queries. Leave the application-side SET statements in place so the proxy can remove the duplicates.
choices.explanation: The proxy does not remove SET statements sent by the application, so the statements are still sent and the cause of pinning remains.

choices.text: Keep the client-side SET statements and only shorten the time clients wait to borrow backend connections.
choices.explanation: Changing the wait time does not reduce unnecessary SET statements or improve the proportion of connections that can be reused.

choices.text: Register the required SET statements as RDS Proxy initialization queries and remove the same statements from the application's connection logic.
choices.explanation: This provides consistent initial settings while removing the per-client initialization statements that interfere with reuse.

choices.text: Skip initialization queries, attach only a pinning filter, and remove the client-side SET statements.
choices.explanation: The filter affects pinning conditions. It does not set the required values on each backend connection.

source.label: Amazon RDS — RDS Proxyの初期化クエリとピン留めフィルター

learning.reason: Move the shared SET statements into proxy initialization queries and remove them from the application. They run once when a new backend connection is opened, helping prevent pinning caused by per-client SET statements.
learning.concept: Initialization queries do not remove SET statements sent by clients. A pinning filter does not make SET statements sent over the network disappear. Move settings into initialization queries when all clients can share the same values.

sourceLabel: Amazon RDS — RDS Proxy initialization queries and pinning filters

title: Start each AWS Batch aggregation as soon as its matching input transformation finishes
prompt: Use AWS Batch to transform and aggregate each of 2,000 inputs. For example, aggregation for input 27 must wait for transformation of input 27 to succeed, but it must not wait for transformations of other inputs to finish. Child jobs in both stages reuse the same job definition, and you want to submit just one parent job per stage. How should you configure the jobs?

choices.text: Create two array jobs and make the aggregation job depend on the overall success of the transformation parent job.
choices.explanation: This preserves input-to-input alignment, but aggregation cannot start until the slowest transformation has finished.

choices.text: Create two array jobs and specify SEQUENTIAL for each.
choices.explanation: This serializes child jobs within each stage; it does not make a job in one stage wait for the success of the matching index in the other stage.

choices.text: Submit 4,000 ordinary jobs individually and specify the transformation job ID for each aggregation job.
choices.explanation: This can create the required dependencies, but it does not meet the requirement to submit one parent job per stage.

choices.text: Submit transformation and aggregation as array jobs with 2,000 elements each, and specify an N_TO_N dependency from the aggregation job to the transformation job.
choices.explanation: Each aggregation job becomes runnable once the transformation job with the matching index succeeds; it does not wait for other inputs to finish.

source.label: AWS Batch — 配列ジョブとN_TO_N依存関係

learning.reason: Use two array jobs with the same size and input mapping. Specify an N_TO_N dependency on the transformation array job for the aggregation array job, so each aggregation child waits for its corresponding transformation child to succeed.
learning.concept: Each container can identify its zero-based index with AWS_BATCH_JOB_ARRAY_INDEX. N_TO_N links matching indices across arrays, while SEQUENTIAL runs jobs in order within a single array.

sourceLabel: AWS Batch — array jobs and N_TO_N dependencies

title: Wait a fixed time for Spot when launching a new EMR cluster, then continue with On-Demand
prompt: A new Amazon EMR on EC2 cluster is created each time for a nightly Spark job. Multiple compatible instance types can be used for task nodes. Normally, you want to launch with Spot capacity, then continue launching with On-Demand capacity for any shortfall if Spot capacity cannot be obtained within 15 minutes. No external retry control will be added. Which configuration meets the requirement?

choices.text: Add more Spot options to the instance fleet and set the launch-timeout action to terminate the cluster.
choices.explanation: Diversifying options can help, but the cluster terminates after 15 minutes, so launch cannot continue with On-Demand capacity.

choices.text: Use multiple Spot options in the task instance fleet, set the launch procurement timeout to 15 minutes, and set the action to SWITCH_TO_ON_DEMAND.
choices.explanation: When launching a new cluster, this prioritizes Spot and switches procurement of any remaining capacity to On-Demand after the specified time.

choices.text: Use an instance fleet with only Spot and increase the maximum capacity for managed scaling after the cluster launches.
choices.explanation: Configuring cluster scaling after launch does not change the purchase option used when Spot capacity is unavailable during startup.

choices.text: Set the entire required capacity for the task instance fleet as the On-Demand target and set the Spot target to 0.
choices.explanation: The cluster can launch, but this does not prioritize Spot when capacity is normally available.

source.label: Amazon EMR — クラスタ起動時のプロビジョニングタイムアウト

learning.reason: For the task instance fleet, specify multiple candidate types and a Spot target capacity, then configure the launch-time Spot procurement timeout and the switch to On-Demand.
learning.concept: The Spot procurement timeout switch used at launch applies to provisioning a new cluster. The same mechanism does not necessarily switch to On-Demand during cluster resizing.

sourceLabel: Amazon EMR — provisioning timeout at cluster launch

title: Set the number of SQS workers from a queue-wait target
prompt: A homogeneous fleet of EC2 Auto Scaling workers processes SQS messages, and each instance completes one message in an average of 0.5 seconds. The target queue wait time is 30 seconds. CPU on an individual EC2 instance is not a useful load metric. Which target-tracking metric should be used to adjust the desired capacity automatically?

choices.text: Set the total number of visible messages in the queue to a target of 60.
choices.explanation: Sixty is the target per instance; applying it to the whole queue fixes the desired backlog at a one-instance value even when multiple instances are running.

choices.text: Use visible messages divided by the number of running instances, with a target of 60 messages per instance.
choices.explanation: This relates the processing rate and wait-time target to a backlog threshold per currently running worker.

choices.text: Set the number of in-flight, invisible messages to a target of 60.
choices.explanation: The number of messages already being processed does not directly measure the work still waiting in the queue.

choices.text: Use only average CPU utilization as the target, without using the queue depth.
choices.explanation: For this workload, CPU utilization does not represent the waiting workload, so this would not control scaling against the requested wait-time target.

source.label: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling — SQSキューに基づくスケーリング

learning.reason: Divide the number of visible messages by the number of running instances, and set the per-instance target to 30 seconds ÷ 0.5 seconds, or 60 messages.
learning.concept: A wait-time target and one instance’s processing rate can define an appropriate backlog per instance. Queue depth alone does not account for the current processing capacity.

sourceLabel: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling — Scaling based on an SQS queue

title: Provide point-in-time data without consuming production DynamoDB read capacity
prompt: An analytics team needs the contents of a large production DynamoDB table, which continues to receive updates, as of midnight selected through PITR, for use in S3. The design must not Scan the production table for analytics or consume its read capacity. How can this be done without temporarily creating another DynamoDB table?

choices.text: Run many parallel Scan operations across the production table and save the output to S3.
choices.explanation: Scan uses the production table’s read capacity and does not provide a single point-in-time copy while updates continue.

choices.text: Restore a separate table using PITR, then Scan that table and export the results to S3.
choices.explanation: This limits impact on production, but it does not meet the requirement to avoid creating a temporary table.

choices.text: Run a full DynamoDB export to S3 for the selected point in time.
choices.explanation: This exports the data within the recovery period directly to S3 without consuming the production table’s read capacity.

choices.text: Subscribe to DynamoDB Streams now and use the events to obtain the entire existing table as it stood at midnight.
choices.explanation: A stream records changes; by itself it does not export the entire existing table at a specified past point in time.

source.label: Amazon DynamoDB — S3へのテーブルエクスポート

learning.reason: Specify the target time and run a full export from DynamoDB to S3. This uses PITR and does not consume production read capacity.
learning.concept: DynamoDB export uses restored data in storage. It is distinct from Scan and from restoring a table after a failure.

sourceLabel: Amazon DynamoDB — Exporting a table to S3

title: Reduce transfer volume after the first copy from an existing NFS source to S3
prompt: A large analytics dataset on an on-premises NFS file system is copied repeatedly to S3 in AWS. The first run must transfer everything; later runs should send only new or changed files to reduce network usage. An appropriate DataSync agent can be deployed for the source, and no custom change-tracking ledger should be built. What should be configured?

choices.text: Choose the all-data transfer mode in DataSync and run it the same way after the first copy.
choices.explanation: This transfers everything without comparison, so later runs do not limit network usage to changed data.

choices.text: Use S3 Batch Replication to synchronize the original files on the on-premises NFS system that are not present in the bucket.
choices.explanation: S3 replication operates on objects in S3 buckets and does not use NFS directly as its source.

choices.text: Set up only an SFTP server and assume it will automatically compare transferred files with the NFS source.
choices.explanation: A file-transfer endpoint alone does not compare NFS with existing S3 objects or perform recurring copies.

choices.text: Create a DataSync task from NFS to S3 and use the mode that transfers changed data.
choices.explanation: After the initial transfer, it can compare and transfer changed data, avoiding a full copy on every run.

source.label: AWS DataSync — 変更のあったデータの転送

learning.reason: Register NFS and S3 as DataSync locations and use the mode that transfers changed data.
learning.concept: Changed-data transfer copies the selected data on the first run and bases later transfers on differences between the source and destination. TransferMode ALL sends everything without comparison.

title: Reduce OpenSearch cluster-management load while search nodes have spare capacity
prompt: With OpenSearch Service, index and node management operations are becoming slow. The data nodes that handle search have spare capacity, but monitoring shows that the CPU and heap of the three existing dedicated master nodes are already saturated. The required index configuration must be preserved. Which capacity should be reviewed first?

choices.text: Keep the number of dedicated master nodes the same and review the dedicated master node type.
choices.explanation: This can increase CPU and memory capacity on the saturated cluster-management side.

choices.text: Add search data nodes only and keep the dedicated master configuration unchanged.
choices.explanation: This does not increase the CPU or heap capacity of the saturated dedicated master nodes.

choices.text: Add a CloudFront cache for search results and leave the dedicated master configuration unchanged.
choices.explanation: This may reduce some external search requests, but managing cluster state for indexes and nodes is a separate workload.

choices.text: Increase only the EBS capacity of the data nodes.
choices.explanation: This adds data-storage capacity but does not increase dedicated master CPU or heap.

source.label: Amazon OpenSearch Service — 専用マスターノード

learning.reason: Change the dedicated master nodes to supported instance types with more CPU and memory capacity.
learning.concept: Dedicated master nodes manage and distribute cluster state. Their workload differs from that of data nodes, which handle search and storage.

sourceLabel: Amazon OpenSearch Service — Dedicated master nodes

title: Reduce request buildup on an ALB when processing times vary
prompt: A single ALB target group sends image-processing requests to warmed-up EC2 instances with nearly identical performance. Short requests are common, while processing large assets takes longer. The targets have similar error rates, but with an equal number of requests distributed in turn, in-flight requests build up on some targets. Client affinity is not needed. Which setting should be changed?

choices.text: Keep round robin and increase the slow start duration.
choices.explanation: This adjusts how quickly traffic increases to newly registered targets. It does not respond to an imbalance in in-flight requests across existing targets.

choices.text: Use weighted random and enable anomaly mitigation in Automatic Target Weights.
choices.explanation: This primarily reduces traffic to targets that show anomalous error behavior. It does not distribute requests based on the number of in-flight requests.

choices.text: Switch to Least outstanding requests and do not use sticky sessions.
choices.explanation: New requests are assigned to targets with fewer requests currently being processed.

choices.text: Add per-subscriber sticky sessions to standard round robin.
choices.explanation: This keeps a client on the same target and does not assign requests based on the target's in-flight request count.

source.label: Elastic Load Balancing — ALBターゲットグループのルーティング

learning.reason: Least outstanding requests prioritizes targets with fewer in-flight requests. It is suitable when processing times vary and concurrent load becomes uneven across targets.
learning.concept: An algorithm based on fewer outstanding requests does not predict remaining processing time. Its purpose also differs from sticky sessions, which keep an existing client on a specific target, and slow start, which controls traffic during startup.

sourceLabel: Elastic Load Balancing — ALB target group routing

title: Strongly consistent queries for the same account's items in a different order
prompt: For a new DynamoDB table, use the account ID as the partition key and the transaction ID as the sort key. A reconciliation process sorts transactions for the same account by status and update time, and uses a key condition to Query only the requested status and time range. It needs newly written data to appear immediately, and each account's item collection stays under 10 GB. Which design should be added when creating the table?

choices.text: Create an LSI with the same account ID as the partition key and a concatenated status and update time attribute as the sort key, then Query with strong consistency.
choices.explanation: This uses a composite sort key while narrowing the range by account ID, and the index supports strongly consistent queries.

choices.text: Create a GSI with account ID as the partition key and the concatenated attribute as the sort key, then set ConsistentRead to true.
choices.explanation: The key condition can be expressed, but strong consistency cannot be specified for reads from a GSI.

choices.text: Keep the account ID and transaction ID keys on the base table and use only a filter expression for status and time.
choices.explanation: A filter is applied after reading. This does not meet the requirement to use sort key conditions for status and time range.

choices.text: Use status as the GSI partition key and update time as its sort key, then select the account ID with a filter on the results.
choices.explanation: The target account cannot be specified as a key condition, and a GSI does not provide strongly consistent reads.

source.label: Amazon DynamoDB — LSIとGSIの比較

learning.reason: Create an LSI that shares the account ID partition key and uses an attribute combining status with a fixed-format update time as its sort key. This allows a strongly consistent Query with sort key conditions for the requested status and time range.
learning.concept: An LSI shares the base table's partition key and is defined when the table is created. A GSI can use different keys, but reads from a GSI are eventually consistent.

sourceLabel: Amazon DynamoDB — Comparing LSIs and GSIs

title: Increase memory per Glue Spark worker while keeping its CPU count
prompt: In a supported AWS Glue Region, a Glue 5.0 Spark batch job is running. It currently uses G.1X workers. Stage parallelism and CPU are sufficient, but executors run out of memory during a large join. You want to keep the current worker count and 4 vCPU per worker while increasing each worker's memory to 32 GB. Which setting is appropriate?

choices.text: Switch to G.2X and keep the worker count unchanged.
choices.explanation: This provides 32 GB, but each worker has 8 vCPU, which does not meet the requirement.

choices.text: Switch to R.1X and keep the worker count unchanged.
choices.explanation: This provides 32 GB of memory while retaining 4 vCPU.

choices.text: Keep G.1X and double the worker count.
choices.explanation: This increases total cluster memory, but each worker still has 16 GB, and the worker count would not remain unchanged.

choices.text: Switch to R.2X and reduce the worker count so the cluster has the same total vCPU count.
choices.explanation: The worker count and CPU count per worker would not be preserved.

source.label: AWS Glue — ワーカータイプのCPUとメモリ

learning.reason: R.1X provides 4 vCPU and 32 GB of memory. It increases memory per worker while keeping the same worker count and vCPU count as G.1X.
learning.concept: G types are general purpose, while R types are memory optimized. Compare CPU and memory per worker, and confirm that the worker type is available for the Region and Glue version in use.

sourceLabel: AWS Glue — Worker type CPU and memory

title: Increase only Lambda’s ephemeral storage
prompt: Lambda transforms compressed files from S3 and stores intermediate files of up to about 3 GiB in the execution environment’s /tmp directory. There is ample timeout, memory, and CPU capacity, and the files do not need to be shared with other invocations or retained after the execution environment ends. Which solution meets these requirements without changing the existing function’s paths or libraries and without adding a network connection?

choices.text: Increase the function’s memory. Leave the /tmp size setting and temporary-file paths unchanged.
choices.explanation: Memory and ephemeral storage are configured separately, so changing only the memory does not increase /tmp capacity.

choices.text: Mount EFS and move the intermediate files to the mount path.
choices.explanation: This can accommodate large intermediate files, but it does not meet the requirements to avoid a network connection and changing the application’s write destination.

choices.text: Change the transformation code in Lambda to store all temporary files in S3 using multipart uploads.
choices.explanation: This is an alternative design that reduces disk usage, but it does not meet the requirement to keep using /tmp without changing the existing transformation logic and paths.

choices.text: Increase the function’s ephemeral storage setting to 4,096 MB, with some headroom, and keep using the existing /tmp directory.
choices.explanation: This changes only a setting and provides enough capacity for the current intermediate files and working space.

source.label: AWS Lambda — 一時ストレージの設定

learning.reason: Increase Lambda’s ephemeral storage to accommodate the intermediate files and working space. Continue using /tmp without adding network storage.
learning.concept: In Lambda, /tmp ephemeral storage can be configured from 512 MB to 10,240 MB. The storage is isolated to each execution environment, and files from previous invocations may remain while that environment is reused.

title: Remove the cause of the backup VPN being preferred during normal operation
prompt: A VPC has a virtual private gateway with both a Direct Connect private virtual interface and a dynamic Site-to-Site VPN active. Traffic from the VPC to on-premises 10.20.1.0/24 uses the VPN even while the dedicated connection is healthy. Direct Connect advertises 10.20.0.0/16, while the VPN advertises 10.20.0.0/16 and 10.20.1.0/24 through BGP. There are no overlapping static routes. What should be done on the AWS side so that the traffic uses the dedicated connection during normal operation and the VPN if the dedicated connection fails?

choices.text: Lengthen the AS path for the /24 advertised by the VPN, while advertising only the /16 over the dedicated connection.
choices.explanation: The VPN's /24 is preferred by longest-prefix match, so changing the path length alone will not fix the issue.

choices.text: Advertise the broader 10.0.0.0/8 prefix from the dedicated connection as well.
choices.explanation: The VPN's /24 would still be the more specific route.

choices.text: Also advertise the target /24 through BGP from the dedicated connection, while keeping the VPN advertisement.
choices.explanation: For prefixes of the same length, the virtual private gateway prefers the Direct Connect BGP route. If that route is withdrawn, it can use the VPN route.

choices.text: Remove all advertisements for the target routes from the VPN.
choices.explanation: Traffic could use the dedicated connection during normal operation, but there would be no backup route after the dedicated route is lost.

source.label: AWS Site-to-Site VPN — 仮想プライベートゲートウェイの経路優先順位

learning.reason: Also advertise 10.20.1.0/24 from the dedicated connection. Longest-prefix matching makes the identical /24 routes from both connections candidates, and for the same prefix the virtual private gateway prefers the Direct Connect BGP route over the VPN route.
learning.concept: The existing VPN /24 is more specific than the dedicated connection's /16, so it is selected even when both connections are healthy. Changing the AS path alone cannot override longest-prefix matching or change the preference between routes for the same prefix.

sourceLabel: AWS Site-to-Site VPN — Route priority with a virtual private gateway

title: Replay outage-period events to only the affected rule
prompt: An order-related EventBridge event bus has rules for the sales ledger and notifications. Event delivery to both rules succeeded, but a defect in the ledger-side processing left two hours of data unapplied. Order events had already been stored in an archive on the same bus before the outage, and the fixed ledger-side processor can identify duplicate events. How can only the outage-period events be processed again without rerunning the rule that already sent notifications?

choices.text: Read the ledger target's dead-letter queue again. Do not replay the event bus.
choices.explanation: The events were delivered to the ledger target, so the queue for delivery failures may not contain the order events needed.

choices.text: Specify the time range and replay to the original bus, targeting all rules.
choices.explanation: This narrows the time range, but the events are also sent to the notification rule.

choices.text: Specify the time range and replay to a separate recovery-only event bus.
choices.explanation: An EventBridge replay sends events to the original event bus associated with the archive; a different bus cannot be specified.

choices.text: Replay to the original event bus for the outage time range and select only the ledger rule.
choices.explanation: This narrows both the time range and the rules, so the ledger can be reprocessed without resending events to the notification rule.

source.label: Amazon EventBridge — アーカイブ済みイベントのリプレイ

learning.reason: Replay the archive to its original event bus for the outage time range. Specify which rules apply and select only the ledger rule.
learning.concept: The destination for a replay is the event bus associated with the archive. An archive created after the outage cannot reproduce past events that were not saved.

title: Keep the S3 archive original and read it only during the audit window
prompt: Invoices are stored in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. For this month's audit, a particular invoice must be readable for one week. The temporary retrieval copy should become unavailable automatically, while the original archived object remains under its original key and storage class. There is no lifecycle rule that deletes the object. Which operation is appropriate?

choices.text: Set a bucket lifecycle rule to expire the object after 7 days.
choices.explanation: This changes the object's expiration; it does not retrieve a temporary copy while retaining the original.

choices.text: Set Days to 7 in RestoreObject for the object, then read it under its original key after the restore completes.
choices.explanation: The restored temporary copy can be read for a limited period while the original archive's key and storage class are retained.

choices.text: Choose Bulk as the retrieval option when restoring, and do not specify a restoration period.
choices.explanation: Bulk is a retrieval option; it does not specify a 7-day period of read access.

choices.text: Restore the object, overwrite the same key with S3 Standard, and delete the S3 Standard object after 7 days.
choices.explanation: This does not preserve the original archive under the same key and storage class, and it does not use the mechanism for time-limited access to a temporary copy.

source.label: Amazon S3 — RestoreObjectの復元期間

learning.reason: Set Days to 7 in RestoreObject, then read the object under the same key after the restore is complete and available. The temporary copy is assigned the specified availability period separately from the original archive.
learning.concept: The retrieval option that determines how long a restore takes and the availability period of the restored copy are separate settings. If a separate copy must remain online longer, copy it to an online storage class after restoration.

title: Perform a planned switchover of a running Aurora Global Database
prompt: An Aurora Global Database is healthy in both Regions and uses compatible engine versions. For maintenance, the secondary is to become the new writer, and the current replication topology must be preserved without losing writes that have not yet replicated. A brief interruption to writes is acceptable. What should be done?

choices.text: Use a disaster recovery failover setting that allows data loss.
choices.explanation: This may allow the operation to proceed quickly, but it is not appropriate for a planned change that requires all writes to be synchronized.

choices.text: Detach the secondary and promote it to an independent cluster.
choices.explanation: This can change the write target, but it does not preserve the current Global Database topology.

choices.text: Change only the DNS destination to the existing secondary.
choices.explanation: Changing the connection destination does not switch that cluster to the Global Database writer role.

choices.text: Perform a managed switchover while both Regions are available.
choices.explanation: The clusters can be synchronized before their roles are changed, leaving both Regions in the replication topology.

source.label: Amazon Aurora — Global Databaseのスイッチオーバーとフェイルオーバー

learning.reason: Use a managed switchover. The secondary synchronizes before the roles are exchanged, and the former primary remains in the topology.
learning.concept: A switchover is suited to a planned change when both sides are available. A failover can be used during an outage, but may allow data loss due to asynchronous replication lag.

sourceLabel: Amazon Aurora — Global Database switchover and failover

title: Define service health from multiple independent diagnostic results
prompt: Configure a health determination for Route 53 failover. The service has three independent diagnostic endpoints, and the existing health checks return separate results. The service as a whole should be considered healthy only when at least two of the three are healthy. How should this be configured without rebuilding the monitoring endpoints as a single API?

choices.text: Set the failure threshold for one endpoint's health check to two consecutive failures.
choices.explanation: This evaluates consecutive results from the same endpoint; it does not aggregate three independent checks.

choices.text: Set the same weight on all three DNS records.
choices.explanation: Configuring request distribution weights cannot represent service health based on at least two checks.

choices.text: Create a calculated health check with the three child health checks and specify that at least two must be healthy.
choices.explanation: This tolerates one of the three checks failing and marks the aggregate result unhealthy only when one or fewer are healthy.

choices.text: Use only one endpoint to monitor the whole service and shorten the DNS TTL.
choices.explanation: This affects how quickly a change takes effect, but does not aggregate the three diagnostic results.

source.label: Amazon Route 53 — 計算済みヘルスチェックの値

learning.reason: Create a calculated health check with the three health checks as children and set the required number of healthy checks to two.
learning.concept: A calculated health check aggregates the current results of multiple child checks. This differs from a failure-count threshold on an individual check.

sourceLabel: Amazon Route 53 — Values for calculated health checks

title: Recover data across multiple EBS volumes together
prompt: A database on one EC2 instance stores its data and logs on multiple EBS volumes. The database can recover from a consistent crash point using its logs, but recovery can fail if the volumes represent different points in time. For this task, protect the selected EBS volumes at the same crash-consistent point without stopping application writes. Which operation should you choose?

choices.text: Take snapshots of the data and log volumes in sequence and apply the same tag to them.
choices.explanation: Grouping them by tag does not align the points in time captured by individual snapshots.

choices.text: Create snapshots of multiple selected data volumes from the EC2 instance in the same multi-volume operation.
choices.explanation: This protects multiple volumes as a crash-consistent set.

choices.text: Snapshot only the data EBS volume and use the current log EBS volume at recovery time.
choices.explanation: The logs may have been updated after the point in time represented by the data being restored.

choices.text: Attach the same EBS volume to another EC2 instance with Multi-Attach and assume that the additional attachment aligns the backup points in time.
choices.explanation: Changing the attachment method does not align backups of multiple volumes to the same point in time.

source.label: Amazon EBS — マルチボリュームスナップショット

learning.reason: Specify the EC2 instance and create a multi-volume snapshot of the required group of volumes in one operation.
learning.concept: Multi-volume snapshots align the group's crash-consistent point. Whether application-level consistency is also required depends on the design.

title: Cut over a changing database with a brief write pause
prompt: Migrate a supported on-premises database to AWS. Business updates must continue during the initial large copy. For final cutover, writes can be paused briefly, and the application will be pointed to the new database after confirming that the target has caught up with the source. The source settings for CDC are in place. Which approach should you choose?

choices.text: Run full load and CDC with AWS DMS, then pause writes and cut over after confirming that the remaining changes have been applied.
choices.explanation: This keeps production running during the initial copy and limits the final pause to settling the changes and switching connections.

choices.text: Use full load alone and assume that updates made during the copy will also be applied to the target automatically.
choices.explanation: CDC is required to continuously replicate updates.

choices.text: Start CDC alone on an empty target and assume that existing records that have not changed will be transferred automatically.
choices.explanation: Existing data that has never been transferred is not brought over by replicating updates alone.

choices.text: When the initial copy starts, have the application write independently to both databases and cut over without confirming that the target has caught up.
choices.explanation: Writes can conflict, and this does not confirm that the target has caught up with the source's latest state.

source.label: AWS DMS — 継続的なデータ変更のレプリケーション

learning.reason: Use full load and CDC to migrate existing data and subsequent changes. Before cutover, stop writes to the source and confirm that the remaining changes have been applied.
learning.concept: Full load alone does not continuously replicate updates made during the copy. Decide when writes to the target will begin and confirm that CDC has caught up.

sourceLabel: AWS DMS — Continuous data change replication

title: Preserve Pod availability policies during EKS node updates
prompt: Update the AMI for an EKS managed node group. A minimum number of running Pods is set with a PodDisruptionBudget, and that condition must be maintained during the update. If Pods cannot be evicted temporarily, the update should stop; the team will provide more capacity before trying again. Which update method is appropriate?

choices.text: Choose a force update and assume that the PodDisruptionBudget always limits every eviction.
choices.explanation: A force update may proceed without respecting the PodDisruptionBudget.

choices.text: Terminate all nodes at once and rely on automatic placement to meet the availability condition afterward.
choices.explanation: Terminating all nodes at once does not preserve the current minimum running count during the update.

choices.text: Choose a rolling update, and if eviction is blocked, adjust capacity without forcibly overriding the budget.
choices.explanation: The PodDisruptionBudget remains in effect during the update, and the update does not force evictions when its conditions cannot be met.

choices.text: Increase only the Auto Scaling group's desired capacity and treat the existing AMI as updated.
choices.explanation: Increasing capacity alone does not update the current nodes to the new AMI.

source.label: Amazon EKS — マネージドノードグループの更新

learning.reason: Choose a rolling update. If Pods cannot be evicted under the PodDisruptionBudget, do not force the update; investigate the failure.
learning.concept: A managed node group's rolling update respects the PodDisruptionBudget. A force update updates nodes even when a condition is blocking eviction.

sourceLabel: Amazon EKS — Updating a managed node group

title: Stop New ALB Traffic from Reaching an Unhealthy AZ
prompt: A service runs behind an ALB in three AZs, with cross-zone load balancing disabled. An external dependency in one AZ has a problem. The other AZs have enough capacity to handle the workload, and ARC zonal shift is already enabled for the ALB. What should you do to temporarily stop sending new traffic to the affected AZ while avoiding recreating the configuration?

choices.text: Delete the ALB's DNS record for the entire Region.
choices.explanation: This would also prevent access to the healthy AZs, so it would not shift traffic away from just one AZ.

choices.text: Immediately terminate all targets running in the affected AZ.
choices.explanation: This removes the runtime environment to achieve a temporary traffic shift.

choices.text: Only shorten the ALB idle timeout.
choices.explanation: This changes connection duration but does not keep new traffic from reaching the affected AZ.

choices.text: Start an ARC zonal shift for the affected AZ on the ALB.
choices.explanation: This temporarily shifts new requests away from the affected AZ. Traffic can return after the issue is addressed.

source.label: Elastic Load Balancing — ALBのゾーンシフト

learning.reason: Start an ARC zonal shift for the affected AZ on the ALB. For a limited period, this directs new traffic to the remaining AZs.
learning.concept: A zonal shift can temporarily move new traffic away from a specific AZ for the target service. Account separately for when in-progress connections end.

sourceLabel: Elastic Load Balancing — ALB Zonal Shift

title: Protect In-Progress ECS Tasks from Service Scale-In
prompt: Video conversion runs on workers in an Amazon ECS service. After receiving a queue event, a task can run for up to 3 hours, and it cannot checkpoint its intermediate results. Service auto scaling must remain enabled while idle, and only tasks that are processing work must be excluded from scale-in termination. The workers can determine when processing starts and ends. Which measure meets these requirements?

choices.text: Set the SQS message visibility timeout to at least 3 hours and leave ECS scale-in at its default behavior.
choices.explanation: The visibility timeout suppresses redelivery to other workers. It does not prevent ECS from terminating a task that is processing work.

choices.text: Enable task scale-in protection before processing and specify an expiration that covers the processing period. After completion, have the task itself disable the protection.
choices.explanation: This prevents termination at the task level only while work is in progress, leaving idle tasks eligible for scale-in.

choices.text: Set the service scale-in cooldown to 3 hours. Remove idle tasks after the cooldown.
choices.explanation: A cooldown controls consecutive scaling activities. It does not account for each task's individual processing state when choosing which task to terminate.

choices.text: Increase the ECS stop timeout and finish the conversion after receiving a termination notice.
choices.explanation: The stop grace period cannot protect the full processing duration, and this does not ensure that only idle tasks are selected for termination.

source.label: Amazon ECS — タスクスケールイン保護

learning.reason: A service task can enable task scale-in protection before processing, manage its expiration while work is in progress, and disable it when processing finishes. This protects active work without stopping service-wide scale-in.
learning.concept: The default protection expiration is 2 hours, so specify a longer expiration for this workload. Task scale-in protection applies to termination caused by service scale-in or deployment; infrastructure failures or task failures require separate recovery measures.

title: Preserve a Single Producer's Send Order in Kinesis
prompt: A single order producer writes state transitions for the same order to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. The same order always uses the same partition key. The stream has a low event rate, and you want to establish the order before adding a subsequent event. The consumer does not reorder events using a business sequence number. Which API usage is appropriate?

choices.text: Batch records in event order with the same partition key in PutRecords, then retry only failed records later.
choices.explanation: Even with the same key, partial success and retries with PutRecords do not guarantee the records' storage order within the batch.

choices.text: Send each event concurrently with PutRecord and sort the responses by event creation order.
choices.explanation: Sorting responses locally cannot change the order in which concurrent writes were added to Kinesis.

choices.text: Use a different partition key for each event with PutRecord to distribute writes across multiple shards.
choices.explanation: With different keys distributed across multiple shards, the order of events for the same order cannot be guaranteed across shards.

choices.text: Call PutRecord sequentially with the same key, passing the sequence number from the preceding successful response in SequenceNumberForOrdering for every event after the first.
choices.explanation: This specifies strict sequence number ordering for consecutive API calls by the same producer using the same key.

source.label: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — PutRecordとPutRecords

learning.reason: For the same producer writing to the same partition key, pass the sequence number returned by the preceding successful PutRecord in the next call's SequenceNumberForOrdering. This enables strict sequence number ordering.
learning.concept: PutRecords can partially fail within a batch and does not guarantee write order. This ordering applies to a producer and partition key; it does not establish a total order across different producers or keys.

sourceLabel: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — PutRecord and PutRecords

title: Reuse Successful Resources After a Stack Creation Failure
prompt: You are creating a test environment for the first time with CloudFormation. It includes several independent resources, some of which take a long time to provision. If some resources fail because the IAM service role used for creation lacks permissions, you want to keep the resources that were created successfully, fix the role's permissions, and resume the operation with the same template. Which settings and procedure should you use?

choices.text: Create the stack normally and let rollback complete. After fixing the IAM role, retry only the failed creation from the same stack name.
choices.explanation: Completing a normal creation rollback removes resources that were created successfully. The state needed to continue from the failure point is not preserved.

choices.text: Use a stack policy to deny Update:Replace for successful resources. After fixing the IAM role, use ContinueUpdateRollback.
choices.explanation: A stack policy controls actions during stack updates. It does not preserve resources or enable a retry after an initial creation failure.

choices.text: Before creation, choose to preserve resources that finish provisioning successfully. After a failure, fix the service role's permissions and use Retry to continue creating the stack.
choices.explanation: This keeps successfully created resources and lets you retry creation after correcting a permissions issue that does not require a template change.

choices.text: Set DeletionPolicy: Retain only for resources that take a long time to provision. After normal rollback, run a CREATE change set.
choices.explanation: Retaining individual resources on deletion is not a setting for resuming stack creation from an intermediate point. A normal CREATE operation does not automatically adopt retained resources.

source.label: AWS CloudFormation — プロビジョニング失敗時の設定

learning.reason: If you choose to preserve resources that were successfully created when stack creation begins, resources on independent successful creation paths remain. After fixing the external IAM role, you can use Retry to continue without editing the template.
learning.concept: Retry after a creation failure and ContinueUpdateRollback after a failed update rollback recover different states. Reviewing resource differences with a change set is also separate from choosing a failure behavior that preserves resources.

sourceLabel: AWS CloudFormation — Options for Provisioning Failures

title: Restore to a point in time before retiring an RDS instance
prompt: After a business process has been migrated, you plan to delete a single-AZ Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance with 7 days of automated backups enabled. If an inconsistency is discovered within 48 hours after deletion, you want to restore a new DB instance to one of multiple points in time available from the automated backups during the 48 hours before deletion, choosing the point that best fits the investigation. The original DB cannot remain running. Which procedure is appropriate?

choices.text: Retain the automated backups when deleting the instance, then specify a restorable time from the retained automated backups when needed.
choices.explanation: Retaining the existing automated backups allows point-in-time recovery to a selected time within the available retention period after deletion.

choices.text: Take only a final snapshot when deleting the instance, then specify any transaction time during the restore operation.
choices.explanation: A final snapshot represents only the point in time when it was taken. It does not include the logs needed to restore to an arbitrary earlier time.

choices.text: Copy the DB instance's final system snapshot to a manual snapshot, then delete the automated backups.
choices.explanation: Copying a snapshot does not let you use the transaction logs in retained automated backups for recovery.

choices.text: Export a snapshot of the database to S3, then directly restore that data to RDS after the required time is known.
choices.explanation: Exporting a snapshot to S3 creates data for analysis; it cannot be used as input for RDS point-in-time recovery.

source.label: Amazon RDS — 削除後の自動バックアップ保持

learning.reason: Retain the automated backups when deleting the instance. The remaining system snapshots and transaction logs let you restore a new DB instance to a specified time within the restorable range.
learning.concept: A final snapshot is useful for long-term retention and is independent of retained automated backups. After deletion, no new backups or logs are created, and existing records expire according to their retention settings.

sourceLabel: Amazon RDS — Retaining automated backups after deletion

title: Atomically create an order and reserve inventory
prompt: An order table and an inventory table in DynamoDB are in the same AWS account and Region. Multiple orders can arrive for the same product at the same time. You need to commit both a new order record and an update that reduces inventory by the required quantity, provided enough inventory is available. If either operation fails, a state in which only one item was written cannot be exposed. Which approach is appropriate?

choices.text: First check the inventory with a strongly consistent GetItem read, then replace the order and inventory items with BatchWriteItem if there is enough inventory.
choices.explanation: Another order can update inventory after the strongly consistent read. BatchWriteItem provides neither atomicity for the entire batch nor conditions for individual items.

choices.text: Use TransactWriteItems with a conditional Put for the order item and an Update for the inventory item conditioned on sufficient stock.
choices.explanation: If either write or condition evaluation fails, the order and inventory changes are rolled back together.

choices.text: First conditionally create the order item with PutItem, then delete the order only if the inventory UpdateItem fails.
choices.explanation: Another reader could retrieve the already-created order before the compensating delete. This does not meet the requirement that an intermediate state remain unexposed.

choices.text: Run a conditional UpdateItem on inventory, then use a Lambda function to create the order item after processing a DynamoDB Streams event.
choices.explanation: The stream update is asynchronous, so the state in which inventory is reserved before the order exists can be observed.

source.label: Amazon DynamoDB — トランザクションの仕組み

learning.reason: Include a conditional Put for the order item and a conditional Update that deducts inventory only if enough stock is available in TransactWriteItems. This operation can atomically update items across tables in the same account and Region.
learning.concept: Include the condition directly in the Update on the inventory item. You cannot specify both a ConditionCheck and an Update for the same inventory item in one transaction.

title: Recovering when an RDS Blue/Green switchover reaches its timeout
prompt: You started a switchover to a validated green environment in an RDS for MySQL Blue/Green deployment with a 60-second timeout. The pre-switchover guardrails passed, but the switchover timed out because it exceeded the configured limit. What should you conclude about the result, and what should you do next as part of your failure procedure?

choices.text: Assume the green environment has been promoted to the new production environment and immediately change the application's connection target to the name used by green before the switchover.
choices.explanation: The switchover is rolled back when it times out. The assumption that green has been promoted to production is incorrect.

choices.text: Assume the connection-target change continues in the background after the timeout, and do not resume writes to the old production environment until it completes.
choices.explanation: If the configured limit is exceeded, changes from the in-progress switchover are rolled back.

choices.text: The changes from the switchover are rolled back. Confirm that blue is serving production, investigate replication lag or long-running transactions, and then retry.
choices.explanation: A switchover timeout triggers a rollback. Once the cause has been addressed, you can retry the managed operation.

choices.text: Manually promote only the green DB in the existing Blue/Green deployment, then have RDS automatically resume the failed switchover.
choices.explanation: Manually promoting green breaks replication and leaves the Blue/Green deployment in an invalid configuration.

source.label: Amazon RDS — ブルー/グリーンデプロイの切り替え

learning.reason: If the configured switchover timeout is exceeded, RDS rolls back the switchover changes. After a failed switchover, confirm that production is running and investigate causes such as replication lag or long-running transactions.
learning.concept: A normal switchover briefly stops writes, synchronizes the databases, and transfers the endpoints. When a timeout occurs, in-progress changes are rolled back; this is different from manually promoting green on its own.

sourceLabel: Amazon RDS — Switching over a Blue/Green deployment

title: Restore from a recovery account without waiting for a copy
prompt: You are protecting an EBS volume supported by AWS Backup. Audit requirements mandate protection against deletion during the retention period. During a disaster, you want to restore the resource from a pre-registered recovery account and avoid the time needed to copy the recovery point to a separate vault in that account. Which configuration meets these requirements?

choices.text: Lock a standard backup vault in Compliance mode, then restore directly from another account without making a copy.
choices.explanation: Locking a standard vault protects retention. It does not enable direct restores from a shared vault in another account.

choices.text: Use a standard backup vault, then make a cross-account copy to the recovery account after a disaster and restore from the copy.
choices.explanation: This provides a way to restore from another account, but it does not meet the requirement to avoid waiting for the copy.

choices.text: Grant the recovery account permission to use the backup encryption key, but do not share the backup vault.
choices.explanation: Key permissions alone do not configure recovery-point sharing or direct restores from the recovery account.

choices.text: Store the recovery point in a logically air-gapped vault and share it with the recovery account using AWS RAM.
choices.explanation: If sharing is configured, the recovery account can restore supported recovery points without copying them between vaults.

source.label: AWS Backup — 論理エアギャップボールトの共有と復元

learning.reason: Store the recovery point in a logically air-gapped vault and share it in advance with the recovery account using AWS RAM. The recovery account can restore supported recovery points directly from the shared vault.
learning.concept: A logically air-gapped vault includes Compliance-mode protection. You can also consider a multi-party approval process as an additional safeguard if the vault-owning account becomes inaccessible.

sourceLabel: AWS Backup — Sharing and restoring from a logically air-gapped vault

title: Distinguishing ownership of resources created in a shared subnet
prompt: A network account shares a VPC subnet with an application account using AWS RAM. The application account launches an EC2 instance in the shared subnet, but only the network account must be able to modify the subnet, route tables, and network ACLs. Which statement correctly describes ownership?

choices.text: When the participant account launches an EC2 instance, ownership of the subnet also moves to the participant account.
choices.explanation: Creating a resource does not transfer ownership of a shared subnet.

choices.text: The participant account owns the EC2 instance it launches, while the owner account manages VPC resources such as the subnet.
choices.explanation: In a shared VPC, participants own the resources they create, while the owner manages the shared infrastructure, including the VPC and subnets.

choices.text: After the subnet is shared, the participant account can freely modify the route tables and network ACLs.
choices.explanation: The owner account manages the network infrastructure resources in a shared VPC.

choices.text: The participant account cannot create EC2 instances in the shared subnet and has read-only access.
choices.explanation: Participants can create supported resources in subnets that have been shared with them appropriately.

source.label: Amazon VPC: VPC sharing

learning.reason: VPC sharing lets the owner retain control of the network infrastructure while participants manage their own application resources.
learning.concept: Minimize permissions for creating resources in shared subnets separately from permissions for changing the VPC configuration.

title: Configure EKS Pod Identity on Existing EC2 Nodes
prompt: In an EKS managed node group using EC2, only the ordering application should be allowed to read a specified S3 bucket. The operating model must associate an IAM role with a namespace and Kubernetes service account through the EKS API, without adding an IAM OIDC provider for each cluster. The cluster does not use EKS Auto Mode. Which configuration is appropriate?

choices.text: Create an IAM role and add only the application's service account name to the trust policy of the existing node role.
choices.explanation: AWS IAM does not identify Kubernetes workloads through the trust policy of a standard node role alone.

choices.text: Set the role ARN as an annotation on the service account. Use neither an IAM OIDC provider nor the Pod Identity Agent.
choices.explanation: This annotation for IRSA alone does not configure OIDC trust and does not create a Pod Identity association.

choices.text: Install the Pod Identity Agent. Create a dedicated role that trusts pods.eks.amazonaws.com, and associate it with the target namespace and service account using a Pod Identity Association.
choices.explanation: The EKS association lets the workload use the dedicated role, and assuming the role does not require a cluster-specific IAM OIDC provider.

choices.text: Associate the service account with a dedicated role using an EKS Pod Identity Association. Do not install an agent, because it is unnecessary on standard EC2 nodes.
choices.explanation: On the specified standard EC2 nodes, the agent is required to provide Pod Identity credentials to pods.

source.label: Amazon EKS — EKS Pod Identityの構成要素

learning.reason: Install the EKS Pod Identity Agent on the EC2 nodes and use a Pod Identity Association to link the namespace and service account to a dedicated role. The role must trust the EKS Pod Identity service principal.
learning.concept: Both Pod Identity and IRSA can provide temporary credentials to pods. On standard EC2 nodes, Pod Identity uses the agent and an EKS association; IRSA uses the cluster's IAM OIDC provider and an annotation on the service account.

sourceLabel: Amazon EKS — EKS Pod Identity Components
