title: Restricting GitHub Actions OIDC role assumption to a specific repository and branch
prompt: Deploy to AWS from GitHub Actions. The production role must be assumable without long-term keys, and access must be limited to the main branch of a specific repository using the default subject format. GitHub Environments are not used. The OIDC provider is already configured, and the audience is sts.amazonaws.com. Which conditions should the trust policy enforce?

choices.text: Specify the GitHub OIDC provider and pin the aud claim. Allow sub to match any repository and branch in the same organization.
choices.explanation: This limits access to the organization, but still allows other repositories and branches.

choices.text: Specify the GitHub OIDC provider and pin the aud claim. Allow sub to match any ref in the target repository.
choices.explanation: This does not exclude other branches or tags in the same repository.

choices.text: Specify the GitHub OIDC provider, set aud to sts.amazonaws.com, and require sub to equal repo:OWNER/REPO:ref:refs/heads/main for the target repository.
choices.explanation: Restricting the OIDC token's sub claim to the repository and branch narrows the set of identities that can assume the role.

choices.text: Specify the GitHub OIDC provider and put the repository and branch string in aud. Do not include sub in the conditions.
choices.explanation: The repository and branch are validated in the token's sub claim. Changing aud would also make it fail to match the specified token.

source.label: AWS IAM — GitHub ActionsのOIDC信頼条件

learning.reason: Limiting the sub claim in the OIDC role's trust policy confines the external CI role assumption boundary to a specific repository and branch.
learning.concept: Validate the issuer, audience, and sub claim, and do not store long-term access keys in CI.

sourceLabel: AWS IAM — GitHub Actions OIDC trust conditions

title: Draft a Least-Privilege Policy from Observed AWS Activity
prompt: A migration job's IAM role has broad permissions. The same account's CloudTrail trail already contains 60 days of EC2 management events from validation runs, and the job passes an approved, specific IAM role when launching instances. How can you use an AWS feature to generate a draft allow policy from observed activity, then review it before application so launch permissions are not broken?

choices.text: Export every EC2 operation used and iam:PassRole from the findings of an external access analyzer whose zone of trust is the organization.
choices.explanation: External access analysis detects access paths from outside the zone of trust. It does not generate an allow policy from the target role's usage history.

choices.text: Convert IAM service last accessed data directly into a policy and allow ec2:* without checking the EC2 operation history.
choices.explanation: Service-level usage data cannot restrict permissions to the EC2 actions that are actually needed.

choices.text: Generate a policy based on usage in Access Analyzer and replace the existing policy with it immediately. iam:PassRole is guaranteed to be included from the RunInstances record.
choices.explanation: The IAM PassRole action is not recorded as a separate CloudTrail event, so it is not included in the generated policy.

choices.text: Use the 60-day trail in Access Analyzer policy generation. Review the candidate policy, then add iam:PassRole scoped only to the approved role before applying it.
choices.explanation: You can narrow permissions based on observed activity and manually meet the known launch requirement that the generated policy omits.

source.label: AWS IAM — Access Analyzerのポリシー生成

learning.reason: Use the target role's CloudTrail activity in Access Analyzer policy generation, then inspect the resulting actions and resources. Because iam:PassRole is not recorded in the logs as a separate action, add the necessary permission scoped to the approved role.
learning.concept: Policy generation produces a candidate based on activity during the specified period; it cannot infer unperformed operations or every required action. Do not rely on the generated result to identify data-event actions such as S3 operations at the action level or to include iam:PassRole.

sourceLabel: AWS IAM — Access Analyzer Policy Generation

title: Allowing a shared vendor account to make requests only for your organization
prompt: A monitoring vendor assumes IAM roles for multiple customers from a single AWS account. Your organization wants to trust the vendor’s designated role while ensuring that a request initiated for another customer cannot meet the conditions for assuming your organization’s role. What should you configure without sharing your organization’s long-term access keys?

choices.text: Only shorten the maximum session duration of the monitoring role.
choices.explanation: This changes how long the issued credentials remain valid, but it does not distinguish which customer the request is for.

choices.text: Trust only the vendor’s AWS account, without specifying a condition that identifies the customer.
choices.explanation: This cannot distinguish requests for different customers that come from the same account.

choices.text: Trust the vendor’s authorized role and require your organization’s unique sts:ExternalId as a condition for AssumeRole.
choices.explanation: This lets the trust policy check both the trusted principal and the identifier for requests made on your organization’s behalf.

choices.text: Issue long-term access keys for a vendor IAM user in your organization.
choices.explanation: This distributes long-term user keys and does not use the requested role-based approach.

source.label: AWS IAM — 第三者へアクセスを委任するExternal ID

learning.reason: Add the external ID assigned to your organization as a condition in the trust policy, and require the vendor to include it in AssumeRole requests made on your organization’s behalf.
learning.concept: An External ID distinguishes requests for one customer when a third party serves multiple customers. Use it together with a specification of the trusted principal.

sourceLabel: AWS IAM — External IDs for delegating access to third parties

title: Periodically updating key material while keeping the same KMS key identifier
prompt: An existing symmetric customer managed KMS key uses AWS KMS-generated key material and supports automatic rotation. You want to keep the application’s key identifier and permissions, and continue reading stored ciphertext without re-encrypting it. Which setting periodically updates the key material used for new encryption?

choices.text: Enable automatic rotation for the same KMS key.
choices.explanation: The application’s key reference and the key policy remain unchanged, and ciphertext encrypted with older key material can still be decrypted.

choices.text: Periodically create another KMS key, delete the old one, and then decrypt using the same alias.
choices.explanation: Pointing an alias to a different key does not replace the key material used for the earlier encryption.

choices.text: Create a new KMS key, change the application’s identifier, and re-encrypt all existing data with the new key.
choices.explanation: Even if this changes the key material, it conflicts with the requirements to keep the current identifier and avoid re-encryption.

choices.text: Periodically recreate the session for the application’s IAM role.
choices.explanation: Refreshing the application’s temporary credentials does not change the KMS key material used to encrypt stored data.

source.label: AWS KMS — KMSキーのローテーション

learning.reason: Enable automatic rotation for the existing key. The same key identifier can be used with new key material for encryption and with existing ciphertext.
learning.concept: After rotation, KMS retains older key material. New encryptions use the updated material, while older ciphertext is decrypted with the corresponding material.

title: Restricting browser uploads to S3 by key and size
prompt: Members upload files directly from their browsers to a private S3 bucket. An authenticated application server issues short-lived signed POST data, and you want S3 to check the allowed key and maximum upload size. Users must not receive long-term AWS credentials. Which configuration should you use?

choices.text: Check only the size in browser JavaScript before upload, and do not include the key or size in the signed conditions for S3.
choices.explanation: A check displayed in the browser does not restrict uploads accepted by S3 as required.

choices.text: Allow the application’s origin in the S3 CORS configuration and rely on that alone to control the key and file size.
choices.explanation: CORS configures browser origins; it does not replace restrictions on object keys or POST size.

choices.text: Allow public writes to the S3 bucket and protect the target key by not disclosing its URL.
choices.explanation: This conflicts with the requirement to accept authenticated uploads while keeping the bucket private. It also does not set a size limit.

choices.text: Have the application server issue a short-lived signed POST with the allowed key and a content-length-range condition.
choices.explanation: S3 evaluates the specified key and upload-size conditions, so users do not need long-term access keys.

source.label: Amazon S3 — 署名付きPOSTの条件

learning.reason: Issue a short-lived signed POST policy that includes the allowed key and content-length-range.
learning.concept: S3 evaluates POST policy conditions. Design browser-side prechecks separately from the conditions S3 enforces when accepting an upload.

title: Explicitly denying a source at the subnet while preserving application allow rules
prompt: An EC2 instance in a target VPC subnet receives TCP 443 traffic from the internet. The operations team wants to explicitly deny inbound traffic to that subnet from CIDRs that an administrator designates for blocking, without editing the security groups of individual EC2 instances. The existing network ACL has an inbound allow rule numbered 100 that allows a broad range. What should you do to preserve other valid traffic?

choices.text: Add a deny rule for the designated source at inbound rule number 150 in the ACL.
choices.explanation: The matching rule numbered 100 is evaluated first, so the later deny rule is not evaluated.

choices.text: Add a deny rule for the designated source at inbound rule number 50 in the ACL, while keeping the other allow rules.
choices.explanation: The deny rule is evaluated before rule 100, so it excludes only the designated source.

choices.text: Keep the existing inbound rules and deny packets to the designated CIDR only with an outbound ACL rule.
choices.explanation: Outbound-only control does not configure the required denial of inbound traffic from the designated source.

choices.text: Add a security group with an explicit deny rule to each EC2 instance.
choices.explanation: Security groups define allow rules; they cannot provide the explicit deny rule required for this purpose.

source.label: Amazon VPC — ネットワークACL

learning.reason: Make the network ACL associated with the target subnet evaluate the inbound deny for the designated source before the existing allow rule.
learning.concept: Network ACL rules are evaluated in ascending numerical order, and the first match is applied. Security groups do not have explicit deny rules.

title: Restrict all API Gateway entry points to a custom domain that validates client certificates
prompt: A regional API Gateway REST API is exposed to a business partner through a custom domain with mutual TLS enabled. The authentication method and backend of the existing API stage cannot be changed. What should be changed to ensure the partner can reach the API only through an entry point that validates its certificate?

choices.text: Keep the default execute-api endpoint enabled while configuring the mutual TLS truststore on the custom domain.
choices.explanation: Mutual TLS on a custom domain is not inherited by the default endpoint.

choices.text: Keep the default execute-api endpoint enabled and require TLS 1.2 in the custom domain's TLS security policy.
choices.explanation: Restricting the TLS version neither requires a client certificate nor limits the API entry point.

choices.text: Disable the REST API's default execute-api endpoint, apply the configuration, and use the mutual TLS custom domain as the endpoint.
choices.explanation: Calls to the default endpoint are rejected, leaving the entry point configured for mutual TLS.

choices.text: Keep the default execute-api endpoint enabled and update the server certificate assigned to the custom domain.
choices.explanation: Updating the server certificate alone neither controls access through another entry point nor validates client certificates.

source.label: Amazon API Gateway — REST APIの相互TLS

learning.reason: Disable the default execute-api endpoint and apply the change to the existing stage. The partner then connects through the custom domain, which validates the client certificate.
learning.concept: Mutual TLS is enabled on the custom domain where it is configured. If multiple custom domains are assigned to the API, manage every entry point that is allowed.

sourceLabel: Amazon API Gateway — REST API mutual TLS

title: Mask sensitive values in CloudWatch Logs by default and allow unmasking only for a few users
prompt: A new CloudWatch Logs Standard log group may receive accidental entries of employee email addresses and other data. Regular operators must still be able to view and search the logs, while only a few approved users may see the same logs unmasked. Which approach masks matching data by default as it is newly ingested, without changing the collection pipeline?

choices.text: Use a data protection policy on the log group and grant logs:Unmask to every role allowed to read the logs.
choices.explanation: Everyone who can read the logs could remove the mask, so unmasked access would not be restricted.

choices.text: Format the output with a saved Logs Insights query and leave other log-reading paths unrestricted.
choices.explanation: A specific query can format its output, but ingestion-time masking does not apply to logs read through other paths.

choices.text: Associate a customer managed KMS key with the log group and allow each operator role to view the logs.
choices.explanation: Encryption at rest does not configure selective masking for operators who are allowed to read the logs.

choices.text: Specify the relevant data identifiers in a data protection policy on the log group and grant logs:Unmask only to approved investigation roles.
choices.explanation: A data protection policy masks matching sensitive data. Only principals with logs:Unmask can request to see it unmasked when needed.

source.label: Amazon CloudWatch Logs: data protection policies

learning.reason: A CloudWatch Logs data protection policy masks matching data in viewing results, while limiting the Unmask permission controls exceptions for investigations.
learning.concept: Data protection policies apply to matching data ingested after the policy is applied. Reading the original value requires logs:Unmask in addition to normal read permissions.

sourceLabel: Amazon CloudWatch Logs: data protection policies

title: Resolve the standard CloudWatch Logs name privately from on premises
prompt: An on-premises log-forwarding host connects to a VPC through Direct Connect. Private DNS is configured for the VPC interface endpoint for CloudWatch Logs, and routing to the endpoint's private IP addresses and HTTPS are allowed from on premises. However, the on-premises DNS resolves logs.<region>.amazonaws.com, used by existing software, to a public IP address. How can logs be sent only through the private network while keeping the software's endpoint name and the DNS configuration for external destinations unchanged?

choices.text: Create a Resolver outbound endpoint in the VPC and have the on-premises DNS forward the name to its IP address.
choices.explanation: An outbound endpoint sends queries from the VPC to external DNS servers; it is not configured to receive queries from on-premises DNS.

choices.text: Have the on-premises DNS forward the name directly to the VPC's network address +2.
choices.explanation: Directly forwarding queries from on premises to the VPC's +2 address is not a supported configuration.

choices.text: Have the on-premises DNS forward the name directly to the private IP address of the CloudWatch Logs interface endpoint.
choices.explanation: The CloudWatch Logs endpoint terminates HTTPS connections to the service API. It is not a Resolver that receives queries from on-premises DNS.

choices.text: Create a Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC and configure conditional forwarding for the name from the on-premises DNS to that inbound endpoint.
choices.explanation: The name can be resolved using the VPC's private DNS. Other on-premises names continue to resolve with the existing configuration.

source.label: Amazon Route 53 — オンプレミスからのインバウンドDNS転送

learning.reason: Create a Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC where private DNS is configured, then conditionally forward the CloudWatch Logs name from the on-premises DNS. VPC name resolution can return the interface endpoint's private IP addresses.
learning.concept: Inbound endpoints receive name resolution queries from external networks into the VPC. Outbound endpoints serve the opposite direction. Check the DNS path and HTTPS connection path separately.

sourceLabel: Amazon Route 53 — Inbound DNS forwarding from on premises

title: Validate CloudTrail log integrity
prompt: The CloudTrail trail will continue delivering log files to S3. An audit must detect whether delivered files have been changed or are missing after delivery. The existing trail destination must be retained. Which configuration should be used to validate future logs?

choices.text: Enable versioning only on the destination S3 bucket and compare the logs' last-modified timestamps.
choices.explanation: This can help retain history, but it does not validate the integrity of files delivered by CloudTrail using signed records.

choices.text: Move the same CloudTrail trail to a different S3 storage class and compare it with the S3 Inventory object list.
choices.explanation: An inventory lists information about stored objects. It does not validate the hashes of the original data delivered by CloudTrail or the log chain.

choices.text: Enable S3 Inventory for the CloudTrail destination bucket and compare each day's object list and sizes.
choices.explanation: Object lists and sizes alone cannot validate the hashes of the original data delivered by CloudTrail or the log chain.

choices.text: Enable CloudTrail log file validation and use the digest files to verify log integrity
choices.explanation: CloudTrail delivers log file digests that can be used to verify whether logs for a specified period have been changed or are missing.

source.label: AWS CloudTrail: log file integrity validation

learning.reason: CloudTrail log file validation uses digests to detect changes to or deletion of logs.
learning.concept: Combine validation with least-privilege access to the log bucket and retention controls.

sourceLabel: AWS CloudTrail: log file integrity validation

title: Set application-specific EFS roots and POSIX IDs
prompt: Several applications use the same EFS file system, but each must see a dedicated directory as its root and perform file operations with specified POSIX user and group IDs. Which configuration does not rely on client-side UID settings?

choices.text: Give every application the same EFS mount target and trust only each container's UID
choices.explanation: A client UID alone does not configure an application-specific EFS root or enforce POSIX IDs.

choices.text: Use a different EFS encryption-at-rest key for each application
choices.explanation: Encryption at rest does not separate POSIX IDs or file system root directories.

choices.text: Configure a root directory and POSIX user on an EFS Access Point for each application, then mount through it
choices.explanation: An EFS Access Point can apply an application-specific root directory and POSIX IDs.

choices.text: Allow NFS in the security group to separate directories automatically
choices.explanation: A security group controls network access; it does not configure a POSIX root.

source.label: Amazon EFS: access points

learning.reason: An Access Point fixes the root and POSIX user used at mount time, enabling application boundaries on a shared EFS file system.
learning.concept: Evaluate IAM authorization for the Access Point, the file system policy, and directory permissions together.

title: Validate server certificates issued by a private CA on devices
prompt: A TLS certificate for an internal application that is not exposed to the internet was issued through an AWS Private CA hierarchy consisting of a root CA and an issuing subordinate CA. The server certificate chain and names are correct, but new managed devices report that the issuer is not trusted. Which operating approach preserves client-side TLS validation without switching to a public certificate authority?

choices.text: Have the server also present the root certificate in its chain. Do not change the client trust stores.
choices.explanation: Presenting the root from the server does not give the client a basis for trusting the received CA.

choices.text: Distribute the internal root CA's public certificate to the trust stores on managed devices so they can validate the server-provided chain, including the subordinate CA.
choices.explanation: The client can use the internal root as a trust anchor and validate the issuer.

choices.text: Add a CNAME for the host name to public DNS and treat the private CA certificate as a public CA trust chain.
choices.explanation: A DNS record does not add a trust anchor to TLS clients or change the issuer certificate hierarchy.

choices.text: Configure a trust store for client certificates on the application's load balancer and leave server certificate validation on devices at its default.
choices.explanation: This configures the server to validate clients; it does not make clients trust the server's issuer.

source.label: AWS Private CA — プライベートCAと証明書の信頼

learning.reason: Use device management to install the internal root CA's public certificate in the client trust stores. Clients can then validate the presented subordinate CA and server certificate back to a trusted root.
learning.concept: Private CA certificates are not trusted by clients by default. Distribute the CA's public certificate as the trust anchor to managed devices; the issuing private key does not need to be shared.

sourceLabel: AWS Private CA — Private CAs and certificate trust

title: Detect unintended reachability in a changed VPC
prompt: For an EC2 instance in a sensitive system, you want to check whether a configuration change creates a path from an internet gateway to a tagged sensitive subnet. Which setting lets you run the analysis after each configuration change, without sending test traffic or enumerating individual EC2 instances, while treating approved public paths as exceptions?

choices.text: Use VPC Reachability Analyzer to analyze reachability between one source and destination once
choices.explanation: It checks a path between a specific source and destination; it does not satisfy the condition of detecting paths through scope rules and exceptions without enumerating individual destinations.

choices.text: Define an access scope in Network Access Analyzer with matching and exclusion conditions, then run an analysis after the change.
choices.explanation: An access scope identifies paths in the network configuration and can exclude paths that are intentionally allowed.

choices.text: Use IAM Access Analyzer to analyze VPC route tables
choices.explanation: IAM Access Analyzer analyzes access through IAM and resource policies, not VPC network paths.

choices.text: Store only VPC Flow Logs and use them to predict paths resulting from future configuration changes
choices.explanation: Flow Logs record observed traffic. They do not enumerate paths permitted by configuration without test traffic.

source.label: Amazon VPC: Network Access Analyzer

learning.reason: Network Access Analyzer uses access scopes to detect unintended reachability in network configurations.
learning.concept: In Network Access Analyzer, use MatchPaths to identify paths and ExcludePaths to omit approved paths. After a change, run the analysis again.

title: Retain an EC2 instance's in-memory working state while reducing overnight charges
prompt: A standalone research EC2 instance loads a large reference model into memory after startup. No one uses it overnight, but in the morning the same process and memory state must be resumed. The instance to be built supports hibernation, which can be configured at launch. You cannot add persistence logic to the application. Which configuration reduces overnight EC2 usage charges?

choices.text: Normally stop an instance with an EBS root volume, then resume it in the morning with the same EBS volume attached.
choices.explanation: The disk persists, but a normal stop does not save RAM contents.

choices.text: Use an encrypted EBS root volume with enough capacity and enable hibernation at launch. Hibernate overnight, then resume in the morning.
choices.explanation: Hibernation saves RAM to disk, preserving process state while reducing instance usage charges during the stop.

choices.text: Take a snapshot of the EC2 root EBS volume overnight, then create a new instance from that snapshot in the morning.
choices.explanation: An EBS snapshot does not include running RAM, so it cannot preserve process state.

choices.text: Keep the instance running and pause only the application overnight.
choices.explanation: This preserves process state, but EC2 usage charges continue while the instance runs.

source.label: Amazon EC2 — インスタンスの休止

learning.reason: Enable hibernation at launch and provide an encrypted EBS root volume with enough capacity to save RAM. Hibernate overnight; when the instance starts in the morning, the OS can resume the process from the saved RAM.
learning.concept: No instance usage charge accrues while the instance is hibernated in the stopped state. Charges for the EBS storage, including the saved memory contents, continue.

title: Avoid adding compute nodes solely to store SQL warehouse data
prompt: An always-on, provisioned Amazon Redshift data warehouse has enough compute capacity for its current query concurrency. A change to the retention period will increase the amount of historical data, but current query throughput is sufficient. Which design is appropriate if the data must remain in Redshift internal tables and the pricing and capacity model should scale only with the increase in storage?

choices.text: Add nodes that rely on local storage whenever storage runs short, and leave the additional compute capacity unused.
choices.explanation: This also adds compute nodes as storage grows, so the design does not scale only with storage.

choices.text: Keep the same node configuration and use concurrency scaling to expand persistent storage for the data.
choices.explanation: Concurrency scaling adds capacity to process queued queries; it does not increase persistent storage for internal tables.

choices.text: Use RA3 nodes with managed storage, and choose the node count based on query performance needs.
choices.explanation: This provides the required compute performance while charging for the amount of managed storage used.

choices.text: Move historical rows to external S3 tables, delete them from the internal tables, and query them with Spectrum.
choices.explanation: Compute and storage are separated, but this does not meet the requirement to keep historical data in internal tables.

source.label: Amazon Redshift — プロビジョニング型クラスターとマネージドストレージ

learning.reason: Use a cluster with managed storage on RG or RA3, and choose the number of nodes based on the required compute performance. The managed storage capacity scales separately from the compute nodes, and storage charges are based on the amount used.
learning.concept: The service manages the local SSDs on the nodes and the S3 layer for long-term storage, so the application can keep using SQL against internal tables.

sourceLabel: Amazon Redshift — Provisioned clusters and managed storage

title: Scale capacity for quiet and busy periods without stopping DMS replication
prompt: During preparations for a database migration, AWS DMS must continue capturing data changes. The initial load is complete, and the endpoint supports DMS Serverless. There are periods of light writes during the day and periods of heavy updates. The goal is to reduce processing capacity during quiet periods without stopping replication. The latest data must be maintained until the cutover date. Which setting is appropriate?

choices.text: Set both the minimum and maximum DCU to the value required during busy periods.
choices.explanation: This handles peak demand, but the allocation cannot be reduced during quiet periods.

choices.text: Stop replication during low-load periods and resume it during busy periods.
choices.explanation: Replication cannot continue while stopped, and any resulting lag depends on source log retention.

choices.text: Set both the minimum and maximum DCU to the quiet-period capacity, and keep the same maximum during busy periods.
choices.explanation: Capacity cannot scale up to the level needed when the workload increases.

choices.text: Run with the minimum DCU set to the capacity needed during quiet periods and the maximum DCU set high enough to handle busy periods.
choices.explanation: Capacity does not need to remain fixed, allowing continuous replication and capacity adjustments in response to workload.

source.label: AWS DMS — Serverlessのキャパシティ設定

learning.reason: Set the DMS Serverless minimum DCU to the lower capacity needed during quiet periods, and the maximum DCU high enough for measured peak periods. Capacity can then scale with demand while change replication continues.
learning.concept: The minimum DCU is the lower bound to which capacity can automatically scale down; the maximum DCU is the upper bound to which it can scale up. Capacity cannot automatically scale down during a full load, so the question specifies that the initial load is complete.

title: Batch Bedrock inference when results can wait
prompt: At night, tens of thousands of articles must be classified using an existing Amazon Bedrock foundation model. The inputs are independent, and there are no external tool calls or conversations. All results need to be ready in one batch before processing begins the next day. The model and Region are eligible for batch inference and discounted pricing, and the planned processing time has been validated. How can you keep the model while reducing execution costs compared with synchronous on-demand calls?

choices.text: Put the JSONL input in S3, run batch inference with the same foundation model, and save the results in S3.
choices.explanation: This groups the work into asynchronous processing and uses batch inference pricing for an eligible model.

choices.text: Call the same on-demand API from multiple workers and distribute the inputs in parallel.
choices.explanation: This may reduce processing time, but each call is still charged at the same on-demand rate.

choices.text: Unconditionally cache each article's different text and assume every request will be a cache hit while using the same synchronous API.
choices.explanation: There is no basis for expecting all the different input texts to be reused as cached inputs, so this does not provide the assumed cost reduction.

choices.text: Change the inference client to a streaming API to enable conversations.
choices.explanation: This changes how output is received; it does not use batch inference pricing.

source.label: Amazon Bedrock — 容量、パフォーマンス、推論コスト

learning.reason: Put the inputs in JSONL format in S3 and create a batch inference job. This processes independent inputs that do not require synchronous responses, uses discounted batch pricing, and writes the results to S3.
learning.concept: Batch inference availability and pricing depend on the model and Region. Each invocation's result can be matched to its output, but this approach is not suited to workflows that depend on conversational turn-taking.

sourceLabel: Amazon Bedrock — Capacity, performance, and inference costs

title: Allocate shared infrastructure costs to departments at fixed percentages
prompt: In AWS Billing cost categories, the costs for the development department, sales department, and shared infrastructure have already been identified. Finance needs a monthly review screen that allocates shared infrastructure costs between the two departments at 70% and 30%, and allows comparison of the amounts before and after allocation. The underlying data, such as the AWS CUR, must remain unchanged. Which method avoids operating an additional aggregation process?

choices.text: Use a proportional split based on the costs of both departments, letting the percentages change with their monthly costs.
choices.explanation: The percentages would vary with department costs and would not remain at the specified fixed ratio.

choices.text: Create a fixed-split rule with shared infrastructure as the source and the development and sales departments as targets, at a 70:30 ratio.
choices.explanation: This allocates costs at the specified fixed ratio and allows comparison in the details view without changing the underlying billing data.

choices.text: Assign the entire shared infrastructure cost to both departments using ordinary classification rules in the cost category.
choices.explanation: Ordinary classification does not split costs by percentage and show the difference.

choices.text: Change the cost allocation tag values to 70 and 30 and have AWS reallocate shared costs based on those numeric values alone.
choices.explanation: Tags can be used for classification, but numeric strings in tag values do not perform a fixed split.

source.label: AWS Billing — コストカテゴリの分割ルール

learning.reason: Set shared infrastructure as the source, the departments as targets, and configure a fixed-percentage split rule in the cost category. The cost categories details page shows the amounts before and after allocation.
learning.concept: Amounts calculated by split rules appear on the details page. This does not rewrite the underlying data in the CUR or Cost Explorer.

sourceLabel: AWS Billing — Cost category split charge rules

title: Assign only the unused portion of a shared EC2 Capacity Reservation to another account
prompt: Within the same consolidated billing family in AWS Organizations, there is an infrastructure account that owns an EC2 Capacity Reservation and an analytics account that shares it. The accounts have agreed that resource management will remain with the infrastructure account, while the analytics account pays for unused capacity. Instances in use will continue to be charged to the accounts running them. Which action changes the AWS billing attribution?

choices.text: Once the reservation is shared through AWS RAM, the unused portion is automatically distributed equally to the recipient accounts.
choices.explanation: When the reservation is only shared, unused capacity is billed to its owner.

choices.text: Change the cost allocation tag to the analytics team's value to switch the AWS billing account.
choices.explanation: Tags can be used for reporting categories, but they do not change which account is billed for the reservation's unused portion.

choices.text: The infrastructure account requests a billing assignment for the unused capacity to the analytics account, and the analytics account accepts it.
choices.explanation: The unused portion alone can be assigned to an eligible shared account, while resource ownership and billing for existing instances remain unchanged.

choices.text: Delete the reservation in the infrastructure account, then have the analytics account create a new reservation and share it with the infrastructure account.
choices.explanation: This changes the managing account and the reservation itself, which does not meet the requirement that the infrastructure account own the existing reservation.

source.label: Amazon EC2 — 共有キャパシティ予約の未使用分の課金割り当て

learning.reason: The reservation owner requests a billing assignment for the unused portion to the shared analytics account, and the analytics account accepts it. Only the unused portion moves to the analytics account; the infrastructure account remains the resource owner.
learning.concept: Users of the reservation continue to pay for the instances they run. The unused portion can be assigned to one account, and this does not grant permission to modify or cancel the reservation.

sourceLabel: Amazon EC2 — Billing assignment for unused capacity in a shared Capacity Reservation

title: Reduce invalidations when updating CloudFront static content
prompt: A web application's JavaScript and CSS are cached for a long time in CloudFront, and each release requires invalidating many paths. Revalidation of the entry HTML is already configured, and the application must display new assets immediately from newly fetched HTML. Keep the old assets for rollback. Which approach reduces asset invalidation costs while still using the cache under normal conditions?

choices.text: Set the TTL of all assets to 0 at all times and overwrite the same URLs, so the assets are not cached.
choices.explanation: Updates can take effect, but the assets are not cached and requests to the origin increase.

choices.text: Enable only S3 versioning and have the new HTML continue to refer to the existing URLs.
choices.explanation: Creating a new S3 object version alone does not switch the existing cache entry for the same URL.

choices.text: Overwrite files at the same URLs and further extend the maximum TTL in effect at that time.
choices.explanation: This lengthens the time the old content is returned from existing caches and does not switch immediately to the version matching the new HTML.

choices.text: Publish assets under unique names determined by their content, and update the HTML links to use the new names.
choices.explanation: The new HTML can specify new cache keys, allowing long TTLs and fewer invalidations while retaining old assets.

source.label: Amazon CloudFront — ファイル名のバージョン付けと無効化

learning.reason: Give assets new names that include a content hash or similar value, and have the HTML reference the names for that release. Keeping the old names avoids mixing old and new cached content, so invalidation is unnecessary for each update.
learning.concept: Using different file names differs from internal versioning of the same key in S3. You can keep long TTLs for assets and roll back by restoring references to the previous names.

sourceLabel: Amazon CloudFront — File name versioning and invalidation

title: Isolate RDS log writes from data I/O
prompt: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL uses a supported DB instance class and io2 Provisioned IOPS storage. When writes increase, data page I/O competes with transaction log writes on the same volume. You want to place logs on physically separate storage without changing the existing DB instance class or data volume. Which feature should you choose?

choices.text: Increase the Provisioned IOPS for the data volume.
choices.explanation: Additional performance may reduce contention in some cases, but log writes remain on the same storage.

choices.text: Move read requests to a read replica and keep the primary's storage configuration unchanged.
choices.explanation: Distributing read load does not change the fact that the primary uses the same volume for data and write logs.

choices.text: Enable an RDS dedicated log volume.
choices.explanation: Transaction logs can be placed on storage separate from the data volume.

choices.text: Enable Multi-AZ and use the standby's log area as the primary's dedicated volume.
choices.explanation: Adding a standby does not configure the primary's data and transaction logs on separate volumes.

source.label: Amazon RDS — DBインスタンスのストレージと専用ログボリューム

learning.reason: A dedicated log volume can separate transaction logs from data storage in supported RDS configurations.
learning.concept: Increasing capacity and IOPS differs from using a dedicated log volume to separate the I/O path for log writes.

sourceLabel: Amazon RDS — DB instance storage and dedicated log volumes

title: Reduce Lambda startup latency for low-traffic SQS queues
prompt: A standard SQS queue invokes a Lambda function. The function initialization and downstream services have sufficient capacity. Immediately after a forecasted traffic surge, messages waited in the queue while the standard event source mapping increased its ingestion capacity. The team wants to prepare minimum polling capacity while also managing the mapping's scale-up limit. Which setting should they use?

choices.text: Only increase Lambda provisioned concurrency and leave the event source mapping on its standard mode.
choices.explanation: This preallocates function execution environments; it does not change the minimum number of pollers for SQS ingestion.

choices.text: Only raise the maximum concurrency of the event source mapping, without configuring dedicated pollers.
choices.explanation: This changes the maximum number of function invocations from the mapping but does not preallocate pollers.

choices.text: Increase both the SQS visibility timeout and the Lambda function timeout.
choices.explanation: This tunes long-running processing and redelivery; it does not increase poller capacity ready at the start of the surge.

choices.text: Enable provisioned mode for the event source mapping and specify the minimum and maximum number of pollers.
choices.explanation: Dedicated pollers for receiving messages are preallocated, and scaling can be controlled between the minimum and maximum.

source.label: AWS Lambda — SQSイベントソースマッピングのスケーリング設定

learning.reason: Use provisioned mode for the event source mapping to provide dedicated pollers for SQS.
learning.concept: Provisioned mode and the maximum concurrency setting on the same mapping cannot be used together. The poller count controls the upper limit.

sourceLabel: AWS Lambda — Scaling settings for SQS event source mappings

title: Handle gRPC end to end with an ALB
prompt: An ALB with an HTTPS listener will expose a gRPC service deployed on EC2. Health checks must use a service method and determine success from gRPC status codes, and bidirectional streaming is required. Which target group configuration should you choose?

choices.text: Set the protocol version to HTTP/2 and specify 200 in a standard HTTP health check.
choices.explanation: This may forward gRPC to an HTTP/2-capable target, but it does not configure health checks using the specified gRPC success codes.

choices.text: Set the protocol version to gRPC and configure the gRPC method path and successful status codes for the health check.
choices.explanation: This supports ALB gRPC routing, bidirectional streaming, and health checks based on status codes.

choices.text: Keep HTTPS on the listener and use HTTP/1.1 in the target group.
choices.explanation: Keeping HTTPS on the client side does not allow gRPC requests to be forwarded to targets configured for HTTP/1.1.

choices.text: Expose the target's gRPC port through a TCP NLB and check only whether the port accepts connections.
choices.explanation: A TCP connection check cannot confirm that the gRPC method is healthy using the specified status codes.

source.label: ALB target group protocol version

learning.reason: Forward requests from the HTTPS listener to a target group using the gRPC protocol version. For health checks, specify the package, service, method, and expected gRPC code.
learning.concept: HTTP/2 on the ALB viewer side and the target-side protocol version are separate settings.

title: Reduce excess small shards in OpenSearch
prompt: In Amazon OpenSearch Service, daily logs are ingested into one new index. About 240 GiB of primary data is placed across six data nodes each day. The existing template creates 48 small primary shards, increasing the load from searches and rebalancing. You want shard sizes for log analytics to be about 30–50 GiB each and distributed evenly. How should you configure the template for the next index?

choices.text: Set the number of primary shards to 3.
choices.explanation: Each shard would be about 80 GiB, above the specified range, and there would not be enough primary shards to place one on each node.

choices.text: Set the number of primary shards to 12.
choices.explanation: This allows an even distribution, but each shard would be about 20 GiB, below the specified minimum.

choices.text: Set the number of primary shards to 6 and create a new index.
choices.explanation: Each shard would be about 40 GiB, meeting the specified size and even distribution across six data nodes.

choices.text: Keep 48 primary shards and reduce only the number of replica shards.
choices.explanation: The number of primary shards and their size of about 5 GiB each would remain unchanged, so this would not meet the specified design.

source.label: OpenSearch shard best practices

learning.reason: Divide the daily primary data volume by the planned number of shards, then choose the count to meet both the shard-size target and distribution across data nodes.
learning.concept: Plan the number of primary shards in the template before creating a new index. Changing a template does not apply retroactively to existing indexes.

title: Stream a large Lambda response to workers in a private network
prompt: A worker in a private VPC invokes Lambda synchronously and receives up to 30 MB of generated data. It must begin processing the first data produced without waiting for the entire response. It must not connect to the internet or add an intermediate storage destination. The team can use a Lambda runtime and AWS SDK that support streaming. Which configuration is appropriate?

choices.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for Lambda and keep using a standard synchronous Invoke, increasing the function's memory.
choices.explanation: Increasing memory does not change the response-size limit or the all-at-once behavior of a standard synchronous response.

choices.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for Lambda and call a streaming-enabled function from the SDK using InvokeWithResponseStream.
choices.explanation: This preserves a private path to the Lambda API and allows processing each part of the large response as it arrives.

choices.text: Open the Lambda function URL directly from the VPC and resolve the function URL's RESPONSE_STREAM using the Lambda API interface endpoint.
choices.explanation: A Lambda API VPC endpoint does not provide a private streaming path for function URLs. Use the SDK streaming API from the VPC.

choices.text: Invoke Lambda asynchronously and wait for the function output to return incrementally on the same connection to the caller.
choices.explanation: An asynchronous invocation immediately returns an acceptance result, not a stream of the function output.

source.label: AWS Lambda — ストリーミング応答とVPCからの呼び出し

learning.reason: Provide a Lambda interface VPC endpoint and use the AWS SDK's InvokeWithResponseStream to call a streaming-enabled function. The worker can consume parts of the response without waiting for all generation to finish.
learning.concept: Buffered responses have a size limit. Streaming raises that limit, but bandwidth is limited after the first 6 MB, so measure whether the response meets the time requirement.

sourceLabel: AWS Lambda — streaming responses and invocations from a VPC

title: Mitigate source port exhaustion for connection translation on an NLB
prompt: The service registers one backend IP address and port in an NLB TCP target group. Client IP preservation remains disabled. During events, bursts of new connections arrive over a short period. Backend CPU and bandwidth have spare capacity, but the NLB's PortAllocationErrorCount increases. Another compatible backend is available, and clients cannot be changed. What should you change?

choices.text: Keep client IP preservation disabled and change the existing backend instance to a larger size.
choices.explanation: This does not increase the NLB source port allocation capacity for the same destination IP and port.

choices.text: Keep the single current backend and increase the target deregistration delay.
choices.explanation: This gives existing connections to a target being removed more time to finish; it does not increase port allocation during connection establishment.

choices.text: Enable Proxy Protocol v2 to obtain the client IP.
choices.explanation: This changes how metadata is sent; it does not increase the port capacity for the same destination.

choices.text: Add a backend that provides the same service at a different IP address to the target group.
choices.explanation: New connections can be distributed across multiple destinations, reducing the concentration of translated ports on one destination.

source.label: Elastic Load Balancing — NLBターゲットグループとポート割り当て

learning.reason: Add another backend IP address and port combination so the NLB can distribute new connections. Port use is spread across multiple tuples of NLB IP and destination.
learning.concept: With client IP preservation disabled, the NLB allocates source ports. A rising PortAllocationErrorCount indicates translation exhaustion, which should be addressed separately from a lack of target CPU capacity.

sourceLabel: Elastic Load Balancing — NLB target groups and port allocation

title: Increase the write limit for a specific Kinesis shard
prompt: In a provisioned Kinesis data stream, writes to one shard have reached the limit. Other shards and consumers have spare capacity. Several active partition keys map to the same shard, and an investigation identified a hash boundary that would divide them between two child shards. Which operation distributes the writes while preserving each device's partition key?

choices.text: Merge the target shard with an adjacent shard.
choices.explanation: A merge reduces the number of shards. It cannot split keys concentrated in the current shard across two write capacity allocations.

choices.text: Use enhanced fan-out for consumers with the same shard layout.
choices.explanation: This separates consumer read throughput; it does not change the hash ranges used to route writes.

choices.text: Consolidate multiple devices so they use the same partition key.
choices.explanation: This removes key-level distribution and concentrates writes further on the same destination.

choices.text: Split the target shard at the identified hash boundary.
choices.explanation: After the split, the active partition keys map to separate child shards.

source.label: Kinesis resharding

learning.reason: Split the overloaded shard's hash range at the identified boundary so that many keys can be routed to multiple write destinations.
learning.concept: A single partition key is still assigned to one child shard after a split. During resharding, consumers should process the parent shard before its child shards.

title: Prepare a DynamoDB on-demand table for a planned burst
prompt: At the start of a promotion, a DynamoDB on-demand table will immediately receive a burst of writes above its current warm throughput. Load testing confirmed that the load is evenly distributed across multiple partitions and that the service quotas and configured maximums for the current table and required GSIs exceed the target volume. Which setting can be prepared before the promotion while keeping the table in on-demand mode?

choices.text: Raise only the table's configured maximum on-demand write request limit further.
choices.explanation: The maximum is a limit. Raising it when it is already sufficient does not increase the warm throughput available at the start of the promotion.

choices.text: Raise the warm throughput of the table and the GSIs receiving increased writes in advance, and confirm completion.
choices.explanation: This increases the capacity available to handle writes immediately at the configured level. The on-demand billing mode can be retained.

choices.text: Keep on-demand mode and add a minimum provisioned write capacity for Auto Scaling.
choices.explanation: Auto Scaling for provisioned capacity belongs to a different capacity mode; it is not a setting used while retaining the specified billing mode.

choices.text: Make no capacity setting in advance and wait for on-demand mode to recognize the load after the promotion begins.
choices.explanation: The system can scale in response to load, but it does not secure the capacity needed immediately after a sudden increase in advance.

source.label: Amazon DynamoDB — ウォームスループット

learning.reason: Warm throughput for the table and its related GSIs can be raised in advance while retaining on-demand mode.
learning.concept: Configured maximums, quotas, and uneven load across partitions are separate constraints. Increasing warm throughput in advance incurs a charge.

title: Multiplex many small HTTP requests to an ALB
prompt: An HTTP/2-capable browser connects to an ALB with an HTTPS listener. Before the change, inspection showed that the connection between the ALB and browser used HTTP/1.1 and that the load balancer's HTTP/2 attribute was disabled. You want the browser to send multiple small requests concurrently over one connection. The existing HTTP/1.1 backend must remain unchanged. What should you configure?

choices.text: Enable client-side HTTP/2 on the ALB and keep HTTP/1.1 for the target group.
choices.explanation: This enables HTTP/2 multiplexing on the HTTPS connection to the viewer without changing the protocol used for connections to the backend.

choices.text: Leave the client-side attribute unchanged and change only the target group to HTTP/2.
choices.explanation: This does not enable client-side HTTP/2, and it changes the protocol contract with a backend that supports only HTTP/1.1.

choices.text: Keep client-side HTTP/2 disabled and extend the ALB idle timeout.
choices.explanation: This can change how long a connection remains reusable, but it does not provide HTTP/2 multiplexing over an HTTP/1.1 connection.

choices.text: Enable sticky sessions so that all browser requests remain pinned to one target.
choices.explanation: This changes target selection; it does not change the connection protocol between the client and the ALB.

source.label: Application Load Balancer HTTP/2

learning.reason: Enable the ALB's HTTP/2 attribute so that it can use HTTP/2 over HTTPS with a compatible client.
learning.concept: The target group's protocol is configured separately. HTTP/2 allows multiple requests to be sent concurrently over one connection.

title: Switch Regions without taking both offline
prompt: ARC routing controls manage DNS failover between a primary and a secondary. It is acceptable for both controls to be On during a switch, but a normal update operation must reject a state in which both are Off. How can you use ARC to prevent an invalid state transition, rather than merely audit the change?

choices.text: Protect all controls with a single gating rule, and have an operator turn the gate On only while making a change.
choices.explanation: This can control when updates are allowed, but it does not check whether an update made while the gate is open would leave both controls Off.

choices.text: Lower the TTLs of both DNS records and recover from an incident triggered by CloudTrail detection.
choices.explanation: This affects propagation and auditing, but it does not reject an invalid update before it is applied.

choices.text: Use a rule that requires exactly one control to be On, including during the switch.
choices.explanation: This does not allow both controls to be On at the same time.

choices.text: Create an assertion rule for both routing controls that requires at least one to be On.
choices.explanation: This applies a condition to the resulting state and can reject a transition that would leave both controls Off during a normal update.

source.label: ARC routing control safety rules

learning.reason: An assertion rule checks a condition on the update result and preserves the safety condition that at least one control is On.
learning.concept: A gating rule controls when updates are allowed. An assertion rule checks which routing states are permitted after an update.

title: Read confirmed writes across two Regions
prompt: A new order ledger will be built with DynamoDB. It must provide reads and writes in two AWS Regions, and if one Region is lost, writes that received successful responses must be readable with strong consistency from the other. Do not expose an application read/write endpoint in a third participating Region. Which configuration meets these requirements?

choices.text: Create an MREC global table in the two Regions and set ConsistentRead to true for every GetItem request.
choices.explanation: With MREC, if an update has not yet replicated from another Region, even a strongly consistent local read cannot return that latest change.

choices.text: Create independent tables in the two Regions and copy updates asynchronously using DynamoDB Streams.
choices.explanation: If a Region is lost before synchronization finishes, an item from a write that already succeeded might not be readable in the other Region.

choices.text: Create MRSC replicas only in the two application Regions and do not configure a third Region.
choices.explanation: MRSC requires three Regions and cannot be configured with only two replicas.

choices.text: Create MRSC replicas in the two Regions and configure a supported third Region as a witness.
choices.explanation: MRSC can be configured with two application replicas and a third participating Region that does not expose a read/write endpoint.

source.label: Amazon DynamoDB — グローバルテーブルの整合性モード

learning.reason: Create a new MRSC global table with two application replicas and a witness in a third Region. Synchronization across Regions occurs before a successful response, and strongly consistent reads are available from the replicas.
learning.concept: A witness participates in MRSC to support availability but cannot serve application reads or writes. MREC uses asynchronous replication, so another Region is not guaranteed to read the same value immediately after a write.

sourceLabel: Amazon DynamoDB — Global table consistency modes

title: Start replacing tasks while keeping the ECS desired count at 3
prompt: An ECS service on Fargate uses the standard rolling update and has a desired task count of 3; all tasks are healthy. At least 3 healthy tasks must be maintained throughout the update, and no more than 4 tasks may run at once. The minimum healthy percent is currently 100% and the maximum percent is 125%, so the first replacement cannot start when the update begins. What should be changed while keeping the minimum healthy percent unchanged?

choices.text: Change the maximum percent to 130%.
choices.explanation: 3 × 1.30 is rounded down to 3, leaving no capacity to start a new task.

choices.text: Change the maximum percent to 133%.
choices.explanation: 3 × 1.33 is 3.99, which is still rounded down to 3.

choices.text: Change the maximum percent to 134%.
choices.explanation: The limit becomes 4, allowing one new task to start while the 3 existing healthy tasks remain running.

choices.text: Change the maximum percent to 200%.
choices.explanation: The limit becomes 6, which does not meet the requirement to cap the temporary total at 4.

source.label: Amazon ECS — ローリングデプロイ時の置き換え

learning.reason: Changing the maximum percent to 134% gives a limit of 4 after 3 × 1.34 is rounded down from 4.02. This leaves room to start one new task without stopping an old task first.
learning.concept: The maximum percent for a rolling deployment is rounded down, while the minimum healthy percent is rounded up. With a small desired count, a percentage difference may still fail to create an integer slot for starting or stopping a task.

sourceLabel: Amazon ECS — Replacing tasks during a rolling deployment

title: Safely restore part of EFS to the active source file system
prompt: Multiple applications share an EFS file system. An operator deleted a configuration directory. AWS Backup has a recovery point from before the deletion, and the other directories must remain in use. Restore only the target directory to the existing file system and verify it before moving it into place. Do not create a new file system. Which procedure should you choose?

choices.text: Perform a full restore to the existing EFS file system and have AWS Backup automatically select only the target directory.
choices.explanation: A full restore covers the entire file system, so it does not meet the requirement to restore only the specified directory.

choices.text: Restore only the target directory at the item level to the existing EFS file system, then verify its contents in a new recovery directory before moving it to its original location.
choices.explanation: This avoids overwriting other existing directories and lets you verify the restored contents.

choices.text: Create a new EFS file system, restore everything to it, and switch all applications to mount it at the same time.
choices.explanation: This requires a new file system and changes the mount target for other applications that are still running.

choices.text: Choose the existing EFS file system for an item-level restore of the target path and expect AWS Backup to write it directly to its original location.
choices.explanation: An item-level restore still creates a separate recovery directory. Moving the restored data to its original location must be done explicitly.

source.label: AWS Backup — Amazon EFSの項目単位の復元

learning.reason: Choose item-level restore from the recovery point and specify the directory path relative to the EFS root. Set the existing EFS file system as the restore destination, then verify the contents in the recovery directory and move them to the original location.
learning.concept: EFS restores do not automatically overwrite the original location. Each restore attempt creates a recovery directory at the root, with the selected item's directory hierarchy preserved beneath it.

sourceLabel: AWS Backup — Item-level restore of Amazon EFS

title: Prevent concurrent updates from overwriting the same S3 configuration file
prompt: Multiple management services read a single JSON configuration file in S3, use its contents to change another setting, and write the result back to the same key. If another service's update succeeds first, an attempt to overwrite it with stale contents must fail so the latest value can be fetched and the change recalculated. How can this be done without a separate locking store?

choices.text: Specify the ETag of the object that was read in the If-Match condition of PutObject, and rebuild the change from the latest contents if the condition fails.
choices.explanation: If the contents change between the read and the write, validation of the condition at write time rejects the stale change.

choices.text: Retrieve the ETag with HeadObject just before writing and perform a regular PutObject if it matches the value retrieved.
choices.explanation: Another write can still occur between the check and the regular write.

choices.text: Specify an asterisk in If-None-Match with PutObject and use it to update an existing file.
choices.explanation: This condition rejects the request if the object already exists, so a normal update also fails.

choices.text: Enable S3 Versioning and write without a condition.
choices.explanation: This preserves previous versions, but does not prevent stale contents from becoming the latest version.

source.label: Amazon S3 — 条件付き書き込み

learning.reason: Add the ETag from when the configuration was read as the If-Match condition on PutObject. S3 compares it with the ETag at write time and fails the request if they differ. After a failure, fetch the latest value and ETag and recalculate the change.
learning.concept: If-Match lets you condition an update on the version you retrieved. If-None-Match with an asterisk is used to create an object only when no current object exists at that key.

title: Keep new connections working during a database password rotation
prompt: The database login credentials for an application are stored in Secrets Manager, and a Lambda function periodically rotates the corresponding user credentials in a supported RDS engine. The application must be able to obtain credentials that work for new connections even if it retrieves the secret while rotation is in progress. Two logins with the same permissions are acceptable, and the application must not have administrative privileges. Which configuration should you choose?

choices.text: Use the single-user rotation strategy and assume the old password remains valid between changing the password for the same user and updating the secret version.
choices.explanation: After the password for the same database user is changed, new connections might no longer authenticate with the previous password.

choices.text: Use the alternating-users rotation strategy, and give only the rotation function credentials that can duplicate and update users.
choices.explanation: One login remains available while the other is being updated, and the application does not need administrative privileges.

choices.text: Replicate the secret value to another Region and use the single-database-user strategy, alternating between old passwords.
choices.explanation: Replicating the secret does not ensure that an old password remains valid in the same database.

choices.text: Give the application the database administrator credentials so that it can connect as the administrator if its normal user cannot connect.
choices.explanation: This violates the requirement not to give the application administrative privileges. It also does not provide continuity for the normal application login.

source.label: AWS Secrets Manager — Lambdaによるローテーション方式

learning.reason: Configure alternating-users rotation and give the rotation function user-management credentials through a separate secret. The function updates the login that is not in use before switching the application secret.
learning.concept: With the single-user strategy, new connections using the old credentials can fail between the database update and the secret switch. The alternating strategy keeps the administrative credentials separate from the application credentials.

sourceLabel: AWS Secrets Manager — Lambda rotation strategies

title: Reuse initialized EC2 instances after scale-in
prompt: EC2 instances registered as load balancer targets are managed by Auto Scaling. Because data is downloaded to EBS during initialization, launching a new instance takes time. The workload repeatedly scales up and down, and an instance is added to traffic only after its health check succeeds. You want to retain initialized instances removed from traffic during scale-in in a stopped state and use them for the next scale-out. Which configuration should you add?

choices.text: Create a Stopped warm pool and enable instance reuse on scale-in.
choices.explanation: Instances removed from the active group can return to the warm pool and be used for the next scale-out.

choices.text: Use a Stopped warm pool, but leave instance reuse on scale-in disabled.
choices.explanation: The prepared pool can be used, but this does not meet the requirement to retain instances selected during this scale-in instead of terminating them and reuse them next time.

choices.text: Enable scale-in protection for all active instances so the same number of instances is maintained even when demand falls.
choices.explanation: This can prevent termination, but it does not stop instances removed from service and return them to a pool when demand is low.

choices.text: Extend the launch lifecycle hook during scale-out and leave all other capacity controls unchanged.
choices.explanation: This can hold new instances before they serve traffic, but it does not let you reuse instances removed during scale-in.

source.label: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling — ウォームプールと縮小時の再利用

learning.reason: Create a Stopped warm pool and enable instance reuse on scale-in. Instances selected during scale-in return to the pool instead of being terminated, and initialized EBS data can be used during scale-out.
learning.concept: By default, scale-in terminates instances. Keep reusable initialized data on EBS, and check the required pool capacity and health when instances return to service.

sourceLabel: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling — warm pools and reuse on scale-in

title: Prevent only database replacement during CloudFormation updates
prompt: A production database and application are managed in one CloudFormation stack. A regular template update must be able to modify the database while keeping the same physical resource. At the same time, you want to stop, before it is applied, any update that would recreate the database or unintentionally delete it from the template. Do not add restrictions to application updates. Which configuration is appropriate?

choices.text: Set Retain for the database DeletionPolicy and allow all normal stack updates.
choices.explanation: This can retain the original database, but it does not prevent a deletion from the configuration or a replacement that changes the physical ID.

choices.text: Set Snapshot for the database UpdateReplacePolicy.
choices.explanation: This retains a snapshot of the old database during replacement, but the replacement still proceeds.

choices.text: Use a stack policy to deny Update:Replace and Update:Delete for the database's logical ID, while allowing ordinary modifications and updates to other resources.
choices.explanation: This blocks updates that replace or delete the database while allowing changes to the same physical database and updates to the application.

choices.text: Use a stack policy to deny Update:Modify for the database's logical ID, while allowing Update:Replace and Update:Delete.
choices.explanation: This blocks changes to the existing database that should be allowed, and permits the replacement or deletion that should be blocked.

source.label: AWS CloudFormation — スタックポリシーによるリソース更新の制御

learning.reason: Use a stack policy that allows application updates and required changes, while explicitly denying Update:Replace and Update:Delete for only the database's logical ID. Update:Modify can remain allowed for the database.
learning.concept: DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy determine what happens to the original resource when deletion or replacement proceeds. A stack policy can restrict the update operations themselves for a stack.

sourceLabel: AWS CloudFormation — controlling resource updates with stack policies

title: Isolate delivery failures to an SNS subscriber
prompt: An SNS standard topic sends notifications to HTTPS subscribers A and B in the same account. While keeping both subscribers, you want to store only messages whose delivery to A remains unsuccessful after retries in an SQS standard queue in the same account and Region. You do not need to copy every ordinary message published to the SNS topic. Which configuration should you choose?

choices.text: Add the SQS queue as a new ordinary subscription to the topic.
choices.explanation: An ordinary subscription receives notifications that match its conditions; it does not receive only notifications whose delivery to A failed.

choices.text: Set the SQS queue in the RedrivePolicy of SNS subscription A, and allow SNS to send messages to the queue.
choices.explanation: This isolates delivery failures for A at the subscription level; delivery to B does not need to change.

choices.text: Set maxReceiveCount on the SQS queue to trigger on failures for HTTPS subscriber A.
choices.explanation: The SQS receive count is used to evaluate messages in that SQS queue; it does not determine whether SNS delivery to an HTTPS endpoint failed.

choices.text: Set a RedrivePolicy on SNS subscription B and receive delivery error notifications through B.
choices.explanation: RedrivePolicy applies to delivery failures for the subscription where it is configured. It does not isolate failures for delivery to A.

source.label: Amazon SNS subscription DLQ

learning.reason: Configure a dead-letter queue on subscription A to retain messages only when delivery to A fails.
learning.concept: SNS dead-letter queues are configured per subscription, and the SQS queue must allow the SNS topic to send messages. This differs from the redrive configuration for messages that fail to be consumed from an SQS queue.

title: Restrict a KMS grant to a specific encryption context
prompt: Data for multiple tenants is encrypted with a single symmetric KMS key. The encryption context always includes tenant-id, while other entries vary by data type. An authorized operator creates a grant for a recovery role and wants to restrict decryption under that grant to a specified tenant. The recovery role has no other decryption permissions. What should be selected when creating the grant?

choices.text: Allow only Decrypt and set only tenant-id in EncryptionContextEquals.
choices.explanation: This requires an exact match of the entire context at decryption time, so valid data containing other pairs cannot be decrypted.

choices.text: Set no encryption context constraint and allow the recovery role to use Decrypt with the same key.
choices.explanation: The grant would not distinguish tenants and could be used to decrypt data belonging to other tenants.

choices.text: Allow only Decrypt and set the specified tenant-id in EncryptionContextSubset.
choices.explanation: This allows decryption operations that include the specified pair, while other pairs in the encryption context can have values appropriate to the data type.

choices.text: Allow the recovery role to use GenerateDataKey only and set EncryptionContextSubset.
choices.explanation: This limits the scope, but does not allow Decrypt, which is required to decrypt existing data.

source.label: AWS KMS — グラントの暗号化コンテキスト制約

learning.reason: Use EncryptionContextSubset to require the target tenant's pair while allowing a context that contains additional pairs.
learning.concept: A grant adds permissions; it does not restrict other permissions held by the same role. With EncryptionContextEquals, every pair in a decrypt request must match the constraint.

sourceLabel: AWS KMS — encryption context constraints for grants

title: Encrypt newly created EBS resources by default
prompt: In a Region, all EBS volumes and snapshot copies created in the future must be encrypted, even if their creators forget to specify encryption. Migrating existing unencrypted volumes is a separate plan. Which setting is most appropriate?

choices.text: Enable TLS for all existing volumes
choices.explanation: TLS protects data in transit over a network; it does not set default encryption for EBS data at rest.

choices.text: Enable EBS encryption by default in that Region
choices.explanation: EBS encryption by default for a Region encrypts new volumes and snapshot copies by default.

choices.text: Update each EC2 security group
choices.explanation: Security groups do not control encryption at rest when EBS resources are created.

choices.text: Export existing unencrypted snapshots to Inventory
choices.explanation: This provides visibility, but does not enforce encryption for resources created in the future.

source.label: Amazon EBS: encryption by default

learning.reason: EBS encryption by default sets encryption as the default for new EBS resources at the Region level.
learning.concept: The setting does not retroactively encrypt existing resources, so they must be handled in a separate migration plan.

title: Share WAF tokens across related domains
prompt: An organization uses AWS WAF token functionality across several related web domains that it manages. Which setting lets users use a legitimately obtained token only across the permitted related domains, without extending token use to unrelated domains?

choices.text: Replicate the Web ACL to every Region
choices.explanation: Replicating across Regions does not define the token-sharing scope across domains.

choices.text: Increase the CloudFront TTL
choices.explanation: The cache TTL does not control which domains are valid for an AWS WAF token.

choices.text: Change the CNAME for every domain to the same value
choices.explanation: DNS settings do not configure the WAF token domain allowlist.

choices.text: Add only the permitted related domains to the Web ACL's token domains
choices.explanation: Token domains explicitly define the related domains that can share tokens for a Web ACL.

source.label: AWS WAF: token domains

learning.reason: AWS WAF token domains can limit which related domains accept tokens.
learning.concept: Limit token sharing to the domains that need it and combine this with the Web ACL's other inspection rules.

title: Verify signatures without sharing the private key with recipients
prompt: An issuing service digitally signs artifacts. Several verification services must verify the signatures with the issuer's public key, without being given the private key. Which design is most appropriate for protecting the signing key with AWS KMS?

choices.text: Encrypt with a symmetric KMS key and allow the verification services to use Decrypt
choices.explanation: Symmetric encryption does not provide the public-key distribution model used for signature verification and would require granting the verifiers decryption permissions.

choices.text: Use an asymmetric KMS key with the SIGN_VERIFY usage; allow only the issuing service to use Sign, and have verifiers use the public key to verify signatures
choices.explanation: A KMS asymmetric SIGN_VERIFY key keeps the private key in KMS and allows the public key to be distributed for signature verification.

choices.text: Copy a KMS key for each verification service and share the private key
choices.explanation: The private key of a KMS-generated asymmetric key cannot be exported. Verifiers need the public key.

choices.text: Schedule the KMS key for deletion and verify the signature with the deletion digest
choices.explanation: Deleting a key does not provide signature verification.

source.label: AWS KMS: asymmetric keys

learning.reason: An asymmetric KMS SIGN_VERIFY key keeps the private key in KMS and enables distributed verification with the public key.
learning.concept: Use separate key purposes for encryption and signing, and grant Sign permission only to the issuing service.

title: Require encrypted S3 connections for third-party access
prompt: Multiple member accounts in the Organizations audit OU own S3 buckets. Some buckets allow IAM roles from external business partners, and those authorized partners must continue using HTTPS. Which control should be used to deny unencrypted connections made by IAM roles to S3 resources in that OU, without relying on per-bucket configuration?

choices.text: Apply only an SCP to the audit OU and expect it to deny access for external IAM roles accessing buckets in the OU.
